# Nucleus — full documentation

> Nucleus adds native windows, OS integration, and packaging to Compose Multiplatform desktop apps written in Kotlin.

Source: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs

---

# Welcome to Nucleus 3.0

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs

Nucleus adds native windows, OS integration, and packaging to Compose Multiplatform desktop apps written in Kotlin.

Nucleus is the desktop layer for Compose Multiplatform apps written in Kotlin. Compose draws the UI.
Nucleus opens the native windows, talks to the operating system, and builds signed installers, all
from one Gradle DSL. Your app runs as a GraalVM native image or on the JVM.

To build your first app, follow the [quickstart](/docs/start/quickstart).

Paste one prompt into your coding agent and it migrates your app phase by phase. See
[Migrate with an AI agent](/docs/migrate/ai-agent).

## Features

- **Native windows without AWT**, with Wayland support, trackpad gestures, pen input,
  [native views](/docs/native-content/native-views), and [GPU textures](/docs/native-content/texture-view).
- **[Multi-window](/docs/multi-window)**: docking palettes and Chrome-like tabs you can tear off and merge.
- **Two runtimes, one DSL**: a GraalVM native image, or the JVM with an AOT cache (JDK 25+).
- **More than 30 runtime modules**: notifications, tray, dock menus, dark mode, global hotkeys, spell check, and more.
- **18 packaging formats**, with code signing, notarization, and [differential auto-update](/docs/packaging/auto-update#differential-downloads).
- **Native design systems**: macOS 26, Fluent, Yaru, Jewel, and Material. See [Toolkits](/docs/toolkits).
- **One language across platforms**: share Kotlin code and Compose UI with your Android, iOS, and web apps.
  Moving from Compose Desktop means replacing `compose.desktop.application` with `nucleus.application`.
  See [Nucleus and vanilla Compose Multiplatform](/docs/compare/cmp-default).

## What's new in 3.0

Nucleus 3.0 breaks source and binary compatibility with 2.x. Read the
[migration guide](/docs/migrate/from-2.x) before you upgrade.

- **One window backend.** The AWT, JBR, and JNI backends and the `backend =` argument are gone.
- **No Compose Desktop windows.** Open windows with `DecoratedWindow` or `HostedWindow` instead of
  `Window`, `Dialog`, and `Tray`.
- **Callbacks on the UI thread**, and macOS Cmd+Q goes through each window's `onCloseRequest`.
- **Window state API v2** without AWT, in `dev.nucleusframework.window.tao.v2`.
- **Satellites, docking, and tabs**, as an experimental [multi-window](/docs/multi-window) API.
- **Packaging** downloads its own Node.js and adds `nucleusOptimization` and a Developer ID PKG.

Full list: [Changelog](/docs/changelog).

## Talk with us

Join `#nucleus` on the Kotlin Slack for questions, design discussion, and bug reports.
[Request an invite](https://surveys.jetbrains.com/s3/kotlin-slack-sign-up) if you are not on it yet,
then open [#nucleus](https://kotlinlang.slack.com/archives/C0BQYKHBGR0).

## What's next

- [Quickstart](/docs/start/quickstart): build and run your first Nucleus desktop app.
- [Nucleus and vanilla Compose Multiplatform](/docs/compare/cmp-default): what Nucleus adds, replaces, and keeps.
- [Migrate from Nucleus 2.x](/docs/migrate/from-2.x): the breaking changes, step by step.
- [Architecture](/docs/concepts/architecture): the layers under your `main` function.

# Install

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/start/install

Apply the Nucleus Gradle plugin to a Kotlin project to build for macOS, Linux, and Windows from one build.

In this tutorial, you'll apply the Nucleus Gradle plugin to a Kotlin project, so one build
compiles, runs, and packages a desktop app for macOS, Linux, and Windows.

## Before you start

- **JDK 17 or later** on your `PATH`, from any vendor. The AOT cache and the Jewel toolkit need JDK 25.
- **Kotlin 2.4.10 or later** and **Gradle 9.0 or later**.

## Compatibility

| Nucleus version | Kotlin version | Compose version |
|-----------------|----------------|-----------------|
| 3.0.x           | 2.4.10+        | 1.12.0          |
| 2.5.0 – 2.5.18  | 2.4.10+        | 1.12.0          |
| 2.0.0 – 2.4.7   | 2.4.0+         | 1.11.1          |

Pin the Compose plugin to the exact version of your row: 3.0.x does not run on Compose 1.11.x. The
Kotlin version is a minimum.

## Apply the plugin

Apply the plugin from the Gradle Plugin Portal, and use the same `<version>` for every
`dev.nucleusframework` runtime module on Maven Central:

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.10"
    kotlin("plugin.compose") version "2.4.10"
    id("org.jetbrains.compose") version "1.12.0"
    id("dev.nucleusframework") version "<version>"
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
    google()
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
}
```

The toolchain compiles your code. The JDK that packages and runs the app comes from `javaHome`, or
from [`lastJdk`](/docs/performance/startup#package-with-the-latest-jdk).

## Verify the plugin

```shell
./gradlew tasks --group nucleus
```

If Gradle lists the `nucleus` tasks, the plugin is applied.

## What's next

- [Quickstart](/docs/start/quickstart): write a `main` function, open a window, and package an installer.
- [Configuration](/docs/start/configuration): the `nucleus { }` DSL.

---

# Quickstart

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/start/quickstart

Build and run your first Nucleus desktop app, then package it as a native installer.

In this tutorial, you'll create a Nucleus desktop app from two files, run it in a native window,
and package it as an installer for your operating system. You need JDK 17+, Kotlin 2.4.10+ and
Gradle 9.0+ (see [Install](/docs/start/install#compatibility)).

## Create the build script

In an empty directory, create `build.gradle.kts`:

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
import dev.nucleusframework.desktop.application.dsl.TargetFormat

plugins {
    kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.10"
    kotlin("plugin.compose") version "2.4.10"
    id("org.jetbrains.compose") version "1.12.0"
    id("dev.nucleusframework") version "<version>"
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
    google()
}

dependencies {
    implementation(compose.desktop.currentOs)
    implementation("dev.nucleusframework:nucleus.nucleus-application:<version>")
}

nucleus.application {
    mainClass = "com.example.MainKt"

    nativeDistributions {
        packageName = "MyApp"
        packageVersion = "1.0.0"
        targetFormats(TargetFormat.Dmg, TargetFormat.Msi, TargetFormat.Deb)
    }
}
```

`nucleus-application` is the only Nucleus dependency the app needs. Coming from Compose Desktop?
See [Migrate from JetBrains Compose Desktop](/docs/migrate/from-jb-compose).

## Write the application

Create `src/main/kotlin/com/example/Main.kt`:

```kotlin title="Main.kt"
package com.example

import androidx.compose.material.Text
import dev.nucleusframework.application.DecoratedWindow
import dev.nucleusframework.application.nucleusApplication

fun main(args: Array<String>) = nucleusApplication(args) {
    DecoratedWindow(onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication, title = "MyApp") {
        Text("Hello from Nucleus")
    }
}
```

`DecoratedWindow` opens a Compose window with a native title bar. Pass the process `args` so deep
links and file associations reach the app.

`nucleusApplication` has no `backend` parameter, and Compose Desktop's `Window`, `Dialog`, and
`Tray` do not work inside it. See [Migrate from Nucleus 2.x](/docs/migrate/from-2.x).

## Run the app

```shell
./gradlew run
```

For Compose Hot Reload, apply `org.jetbrains.compose.hot-reload` and run `./gradlew hotRun`. On
macOS, also declare `dev.nucleusframework:nucleus.decorated-window-tao:<version>` in the module, or
the hot reload window does not open.

## Package the app

```shell
./gradlew packageDistributionForCurrentOS
```

The installer lands in `build/compose/binaries/main/<format>/`. See
[Configuration](/docs/start/configuration#select-packaging-formats) to add formats.

## What's next

- [Windows](/docs/windows): `DecoratedWindow`, title bars, and dialogs.
- [Configuration](/docs/start/configuration): the `nucleus { }` DSL.
- [Architecture](/docs/concepts/architecture): what runs under your `main` function.

# Configuration

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/start/configuration

Write the minimal nucleus.application { } block a new app needs, then find the page that covers each packaging, runtime, and OS integration option.

The `nucleus.application { }` block in `build.gradle.kts` tells the plugin how to run and package
your app. A Kotlin/Native app uses `nucleus.nativeApplication { }` instead, see
[the Gradle DSL reference](/docs/reference/gradle-dsl#native-application).

## Write the minimal configuration

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
import dev.nucleusframework.desktop.application.dsl.TargetFormat

nucleus.application {
    mainClass = "com.example.MainKt" // fun main in com/example/Main.kt

    nativeDistributions {
        packageName = "MyApp"
        packageVersion = "1.0.0"
        description = "Notes that sync across devices"
        vendor = "Example Corp"
        homepage = "https://myapp.example.com" // required for DEB and RPM
        targetFormats(TargetFormat.Dmg, TargetFormat.Msi, TargetFormat.Deb)

        macOS {
            bundleID = "com.example.myapp"
            iconFile.set(project.file("icons/app.icns"))
        }
        windows { iconFile.set(project.file("icons/app.ico")) }
        linux { iconFile.set(project.file("icons/app.png")) }
    }
}
```

`packageName` and `packageVersion` end up in installer names and OS metadata.

## Select packaging formats

`targetFormats(...)` accepts any of the 18 `TargetFormat` values. Each build machine produces the
formats of its own OS.

| OS | Formats |
|---|---|
| macOS | `Dmg`, `Pkg` |
| Windows | `Msi`, `Exe`, `Nsis`, `NsisWeb`, `Portable`, `AppX` |
| Linux | `Deb`, `Rpm`, `AppImage`, `Pacman`, `Snap`, `Flatpak` |
| Any | `Zip`, `Tar`, `SevenZ`, `RawAppImage` |

## Find the page for each option

| To configure | See |
|---|---|
| JVM, GraalVM native image, or AOT cache | [Runtimes](/docs/performance), [GraalVM](/docs/performance/graalvm/configuration), [AOT cache](/docs/performance/aot-cache) |
| The startup pack (`nucleusOptimization`) | [Startup optimization](/docs/performance/startup) |
| URL schemes (`protocol(...)`) and file types (`fileAssociation(...)`) | [Deep links](/docs/lifecycle/deep-links), [Gradle DSL](/docs/reference/gradle-dsl#runtime-image) |
| Corporate CA bundles (`trustedCertificates`) | [Trusted certificates](/docs/packaging/trusted-certificates) |
| JDK modules and JRE fonts (`stripJreFonts`) | [Trim the runtime image](/docs/packaging#trim-the-runtime-image) |
| The Node.js used for packaging | [Provision Node.js](/docs/packaging#provision-nodejs) |
| Per-OS installers | [macOS](/docs/packaging/macos#choose-a-pkg-channel), [Windows](/docs/packaging/windows), [Linux](/docs/packaging/linux) |
| Signing and notarization | [Code signing](/docs/packaging/code-signing) |
| ProGuard and every other property | [Gradle DSL reference](/docs/reference/gradle-dsl#buildtypes) |

`stripJreFonts` defaults to `true`, and `macOS { pkg { appStore = … } }` replaces `macOS.appStore`.
See [Migrate from Nucleus 2.x](/docs/migrate/from-2.x).

## What's next

- [Quickstart](/docs/start/quickstart): run and package a first app.
- [Packaging](/docs/packaging): build the installers and ship them.
- [Gradle DSL reference](/docs/reference/gradle-dsl): every property and type.

# Architecture

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/concepts/architecture

The layers of a Nucleus application, where AWT still runs, and how native libraries ship.

A Nucleus app is a Compose Multiplatform app. Nucleus adds native windows and OS integration
underneath it, and the Gradle plugin packages the result. `DecoratedWindow` and helpers such as
`isSystemInDarkMode()` are regular `@Composable` functions.

## The layers

| Layer | What it contains |
|---|---|
| Your application | Compose UI and business logic, shareable with Android and iOS through `commonMain`. |
| Nucleus runtime | OS integration, lifecycle, performance and update modules, and `nucleusApplication`. See [Modules](/docs/concepts/modules). |
| Window layer | Native windows, input and the event loop. `nucleus-application` brings it in. |
| Compose Multiplatform | The UI toolkit. |
| Runtime | A JVM (JDK 17 or later, any vendor; JDK 25 with `decorated-window-jewel`) or a GraalVM native image. See [Runtimes](/docs/performance). |

`nucleusApplication` runs the event loop on the calling thread and returns once the last window
closes. Input, composition and drawing share one thread; see [Threading](/docs/concepts/threading).

The AWT backends (`decorated-window-awt`, `-jbr`, `-jni`), `NucleusBackend` and the `backend =`
argument are gone. Compose Desktop's AWT `Window`, `Dialog` and `Tray` are unsupported. See
[Migrate from 2.x](/docs/migrate/from-2.x).

## Where AWT still runs

- Compose starts the AWT event thread, which keeps the JVM alive. `nucleusApplication` therefore
  calls `exitProcess` after the last window closes. Pass `exitProcessOnExit = false` to return
  and keep running.
- Your own AWT code runs on the AWT event thread, a different thread from the one Compose uses.
- A Swing or Compose Desktop host that embeds Nucleus libraries without `nucleusApplication` still
  works. Check `WindowBackend.Current` to tell the cases apart:

```kotlin
if (WindowBackend.Current == WindowBackend.Tao) {
    // Launched through nucleusApplication
}
```

## Native libraries

Nucleus loads its JNI libraries for you. In `./gradlew run`, IDE runs and fat JARs, it extracts
them to a per-user cache; relocate it with `-Dnucleus.native.cacheDir=<dir>`. See
[Native library loader](/docs/performance/native-library-loader).

Packaged apps no longer carry Nucleus native libraries inside their JARs. Code that read them as
classpath resources must load them through `NativeLibraryLoader`.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- The window layer is `decorated-window-tao`, a wrapper around Tao, a Rust windowing library.
- Most runtime modules compile to Java 11 bytecode, so libraries that embed them work on older
  toolchains.
- Skia draws through Metal on macOS, ANGLE on Direct3D 11 on Windows, and EGL on Linux.
- Packaged JVM apps load native libraries from the app directory (`-Dnucleus.native.libraryPath`),
  native images from next to the executable.
- In an AWT host, `WindowBackend.Current` is `WindowBackend.Awt` and native callbacks run on the
  AWT event thread.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## What's next

- [Runtimes](/docs/performance): GraalVM native image or the JVM.
- [Modules](/docs/concepts/modules): what `nucleus-application` brings and what you add.
- [Threading](/docs/concepts/threading): the UI thread, native callbacks and the event-loop watchdog.
- [Windows](/docs/windows): open your first `DecoratedWindow`.

# Modules

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/concepts/modules

The Nucleus Gradle modules, what nucleus-application brings with it, and how to add the rest.

Nucleus modules release together under the `dev.nucleusframework` group. `nucleus-application`
brings the entry point, windows and runtime essentials. Add any other module when your app needs
it, on the same version:

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
val nucleusVersion = "<version>"

dependencies {
    implementation(compose.desktop.currentOs)
    implementation("dev.nucleusframework:nucleus.nucleus-application:$nucleusVersion")
    implementation("dev.nucleusframework:nucleus.notification-common:$nucleusVersion")
    implementation("dev.nucleusframework:nucleus.global-hotkey:$nucleusVersion")
}
```

## What nucleus-application brings

Windows, dialogs, popups and native content, window themes and icons, platform detection,
`NucleusApp` metadata, single instance, deep links, the AOT cache, `isSystemInDarkMode()`, and
[spell check](/docs/os/spell-check). The native macOS context menu, `Modifier.keepScreenOn()` and
native image support also come with it.

`nucleus-application` exposes `decorated-window-tao`, so remove your own `decorated-window-tao`
dependency. `decorated-window-awt`, `decorated-window-jbr` and `decorated-window-jni` no longer
exist. See [Migrate from 2.x](/docs/migrate/from-2.x).

## Toolkit modules

`decorated-window-jewel` (Java 25), `decorated-window-material2` and `decorated-window-material3`
style windows and dialogs inside `nucleusApplication`. macOS 26, Fluent and Yaru live in their own
repositories. See [Toolkits](/docs/toolkits).

## OS integration modules

| Capability | Module |
|---|---|
| Notifications, one DSL for every OS | [`notification-common`](/docs/os/notifications) (brings the per-OS modules) |
| Notifications per OS | `notification-macos`, `notification-windows`, `notification-linux` |
| Dock menu (macOS) | `launcher-macos` |
| Jump lists and taskbar buttons (Windows) | `launcher-windows` |
| Unity quicklist (Linux) | `launcher-linux` |
| Native menu bar (macOS) | `menu-macos` |
| Taskbar progress | `taskbar-progress`, [`taskbar-progress-tao`](/docs/os/dock-taskbar/progress) |
| System accent color | `system-color` |
| Global hotkeys | `global-hotkey` |
| Media controls (Now Playing, SMTC, MPRIS) | `media-control` |
| System info (CPU, RAM, GPU, batteries) | `system-info` |
| SF Symbols catalogue | [`sf-symbols`](/docs/os/icons/sf-symbols) |
| FreeDesktop icon names | `freedesktop-icons` |

## Lifecycle modules

| Capability | Module |
|---|---|
| Auto-launch at login | `autolaunch` |
| Scheduled tasks (cron, periodic, boot) | `scheduler` |
| Scheduler tests on a virtual clock | [`scheduler-testing`](/docs/lifecycle/background/scheduler-testing) |
| File-system watcher | [`fs-watcher`](/docs/lifecycle/fs-watcher) |
| Login items, launch agents and daemons (macOS) | `service-management-macos` |
| Efficiency mode and screen wake locks | `energy-manager` |
| Auto-update | [`updater-runtime`](/docs/packaging/auto-update) |

## Performance and networking modules

| Capability | Module |
|---|---|
| Trust manager backed by the OS certificate store | `native-ssl` |
| `java.net.http.HttpClient` with native trust | [`native-http`](/docs/performance/native-http) |
| OkHttp with native trust | `native-http-okhttp` |
| Ktor with native trust | `native-http-ktor` |
| Linux HiDPI scale detection | `linux-hidpi` |

The three `native-http` modules bring `native-ssl` with them.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- On the compile classpath, `nucleus-application` brings `decorated-window-tao`,
  `decorated-window-core`, `core-runtime`, `aot-runtime`, `darkmode-detector` and `spellcheck`.
- At run time only, it adds `graalvm-runtime` (with `linux-hidpi`), `menu-macos` (with
  `sf-symbols`), `energy-manager` and `angle-natives`. Declare one of them to import its API.
- The notification, launcher and media-control modules deliver their callbacks through
  `NucleusUiThread`. See [Threading](/docs/concepts/threading).
- Modules read your app's identity from `NucleusApp.appId`, `NucleusApp.version` and the other
  properties the Gradle plugin writes at build time.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

- [Threading](/docs/concepts/threading): which thread runs your callbacks.
- [OS integration](/docs/os): recipes per capability.

# Threading

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/concepts/threading

The UI thread that runs Compose under Nucleus, which callbacks reach it, how to port Swing-style code, and the Windows event-loop watchdog.

`nucleusApplication` runs the event loop on the thread that calls it, `main` in a standard app.
That UI thread handles input, composition and drawing for every window, and `Dispatchers.Main`
points at it, so `LaunchedEffect`, `rememberCoroutineScope()` and view-model scopes resume there.

The AWT event dispatch thread (EDT) still exists, but it is a different thread. Code posted to it
runs outside Compose's thread.

## Native callbacks on the UI thread

These modules call your code on the UI thread, so you can update Compose state directly:

| Module | Callbacks |
|---|---|
| `notification-common` (macOS), `notification-windows`, `notification-linux` | Notification activations, actions, dismissals and failures |
| `media-control` | Play, pause, next, previous, stop, seek |
| `launcher-macos` / `launcher-linux` | Dock menu and Unity quicklist item clicks |
| `menu-macos` | Menu actions and delegate events |

These callbacks used to run on the AWT EDT. Code that assumed the EDT, such as
`SwingUtilities.isEventDispatchThread()` checks, must change. See
[Migrate from 2.x](/docs/migrate/from-2.x).

Other modules call you on the thread that received the event. `global-hotkey`, for example, calls
its listener from a native thread. Post to the UI thread with `NucleusUiThread` before touching UI
state:

```kotlin
GlobalHotKeyManager.register(keyCode = KeyEvent.VK_F12) { _, _ ->
    NucleusUiThread.post { viewModel.onHotKey() }
}
```

`post` always queues the block, even from the UI thread, so callback order stays the same.

## Port Swing-style code

| Swing-style code | Replace with |
|---|---|
| `SwingUtilities.invokeLater { }`, `EventQueue.invokeLater { }` | `withContext(Dispatchers.Main) { }` or `NucleusUiThread.post { }` |
| `Dispatchers.Swing` | `Dispatchers.Main` |
| `SwingUtilities.isEventDispatchThread()` | Drop the check, or dispatch to `Dispatchers.Main` |
| `javax.swing.Timer` | `LaunchedEffect` with `delay` |

A Swing `JFrame` can still run beside Nucleus windows, on the EDT. Reach it with
`SwingUtilities.invokeLater` and come back with `Dispatchers.Main`.

## Detect a stalled event loop

On Windows, Nucleus logs `SEVERE` with a full thread dump when a window stops responding. Register
handlers to react, for example to report the hang:

```kotlin
fun main(args: Array<String>) = nucleusApplication(args) {
    onUnresponsive { crashReporter.reportHang() }
    onResponsive { crashReporter.hangEnded() }
    // ...
}
```

- Both handlers run on a dedicated watchdog thread, since the UI thread is the stuck one. Work you
  post to `Dispatchers.Main` from them waits until the stall ends.
- `onResponsive` fires only after a stall that `onUnresponsive` reported.
- Each call replaces the previous handler, so calling them from the application block is safe.
- Nucleus shows no dialog by default.

Wrap long synchronous UI-thread work in `expectUnresponsive` so it is not reported. It returns the
block's result and works from any thread:

```kotlin
expectUnresponsive { importHugeProjectSynchronously() }
```

| System property | Effect |
|---|---|
| `-Dnucleus.tao.watchdog=false` | Disables the watchdog. `true` forces it on under a debugger. |
| `-Dnucleus.tao.watchdogGraceMs=<ms>` | Extra time before a stall is reported. Default `5000`. |
| `-Dnucleus.tao.watchdogDialog=true` | Also shows the native error dialog on a stall. |

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- On macOS the event loop runs on the process main thread, as AppKit requires.
- Nucleus registers its `Dispatchers.Main` with a higher priority than `kotlinx-coroutines-swing`,
  so the Swing dispatcher on the classpath does not take over.
- Outside `nucleusApplication`, `NucleusUiThread.post` falls back to `EventQueue.invokeLater`, so
  a Swing host gets its callbacks on the EDT. `isRegistered` tells you which case applies.
- The watchdog asks Windows every 2 seconds whether each window is hung, sends nothing to the event
  loop, and stays off under a debugger. It reads a poll that overslept by more than 10 seconds as
  a system suspend.
- The watchdog runs on Windows only: macOS has no public "not responding" query, and X11's ping
  would disturb the loop it measures.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

# Windows

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/windows

Open native desktop windows from Compose with nucleusApplication and DecoratedWindow, set their chrome, and route secondary windows through a host.

`nucleusApplication` starts the Nucleus runtime and `DecoratedWindow` opens a native window with a
Compose title bar slot. Both come with `nucleus-application`.

## Open a window

```kotlin
fun main() = nucleusApplication {
    DecoratedWindow(
        onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication,
        state = rememberWindowState(size = DpSize(1024.dp, 720.dp)),
        title = "MyApp",
        minimumSize = DpSize(640.dp, 480.dp),
    ) {
        TitleBar { _ -> Text("MyApp", Modifier.align(Alignment.CenterHorizontally)) }
        Box(Modifier.fillMaxSize()) { /* app content */ }
    }
}
```

`TitleBar` drags the window from its empty space and receives the `DecoratedWindowState` (focus,
maximized, fullscreen). Call `DecoratedWindow` again to open a second window. For custom chrome,
macOS glass, or Windows 11 Mica, use [`WindowScaffold`](/docs/windows/window-scaffold). App-wide
options (single instance, locale, Dock policy, exit behavior) live on
[Application](/docs/lifecycle/application).

Nucleus has a single window backend: `NucleusBackend`, `LocalNucleusBackend`, and `backend =` are
gone. Compose Desktop's AWT `Window`, `Dialog`, and `Tray` are unsupported. See
[Migrate from 2.x](/docs/migrate/from-2.x).

## Set the window chrome

`resizable`, `minimizable`, and `maximizable` default to `true` and react to changes.
`resizable = false` also removes the maximize button, so a close-only window needs two flags:

```kotlin
DecoratedWindow(onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication, resizable = false, minimizable = false) { /* ... */ }
```

On Linux, desktop shortcuts (Super+H, Alt+Space) still minimize and maximize. On macOS the traffic
lights grey out and the **Window** menu items follow. `DecoratedDialog` passes `false` for both.

`minimizable` and `maximizable` are new on every `DecoratedWindow` and `HostedWindow` overload and
on `NucleusWindowHost.Window`. A custom `NucleusWindowHost` must add them.

## Open a window from composition

`DecoratedWindow` and `DecoratedDialog` also exist without a receiver. Call them from a navigation
destination or a row action:

```kotlin
@Composable
fun EditorWindow(onClose: () -> Unit) {
    DecoratedWindow(onCloseRequest = onClose, title = "Editor") { EditorContent() }
}
```

They read `LocalNucleusApplicationScope`, which throws outside `nucleusApplication { }`.

Material and Jewel windows and dialogs lost their receiver-less overloads. Call them inside
`with(LocalNucleusApplicationScope.current) { }`.

## Route windows through a host

A library or navigation layer calls `HostedWindow` / `HostedDialog`. They open through
`LocalNucleusWindowHost` / `LocalNucleusDialogHost`, so the app picks the window type once:

```kotlin
CompositionLocalProvider(LocalNucleusWindowHost provides MyMaterialWindowHost) {
    NavigationGraph() // every HostedWindow below uses this host
}
```

The default hosts draw no title bar: compose `TitleBar` in the content. To theme hosted windows,
implement the `NucleusWindowHost.Window` `fun interface`, and override the
[window API v2](/docs/windows/window-state) overload too: the default drops `maxSize` and
`requestScreen`. `transparent`, `clickThrough`, `visibleOnAllWorkspaces`, and `forceX11` exist only
on `DecoratedWindow`.

## Use the window handle

`nucleusWindow` in the content lambda, or `LocalNucleusWindow` deeper in the tree, returns the
`NucleusWindow` handle:

```kotlin
val focused by nucleusWindow.focusFlow.collectAsState()
Button(onClick = { nucleusWindow.setMaximized(true) }) { Text(if (focused) "Maximize" else "…") }
```

| Group | Members |
| --- | --- |
| State | `isFocused`, `isMinimized`, `isMaximized`, `isFullscreen`, and a `*Flow` for each |
| Geometry | `boundsOnScreen()`: outer bounds in dp, `null` before the window appears |
| Actions | `show`, `hide`, `toFront`, `requestFocus`, `setMinimized`, `setMaximized`, `setFullscreen`, `setAlwaysOnTop`, `setMinimumSize`, `setIcon`, `close` |
| Native | `unsafe.taoWindow`, `unsafe.taoHandle` (replace the removed `awtWindow` / `awtDialog`) |

## Hide a window from the taskbar or Dock

`hiddenFromDock = true` keeps a window visible but removes it from the taskbar, Alt+Tab, or Dock.

- **macOS**: the app loses its Dock icon and menu bar. The setting is app-wide: the last window to
  set it wins. For a menu-bar app, use `dockIconFollowsWindows = true` instead. See
  [Hide the Dock icon on macOS](/docs/os/tray/tray-app#hide-the-dock-icon-on-macos).
- **Linux**: native Wayland ignores it. Pass `forceX11 = true` or see
  [Linux and Wayland](/docs/windows/linux-wayland).

## Text input

IME composition reaches Compose text fields as preedit on every platform, and the candidate window
follows the caret. Keys the IME consumes don't reach the text field.

## Handle uncaught exceptions

An exception that escapes a window event is fatal: Nucleus logs it, shows an error dialog, and
exits with code 1 (`exitProcessOnExit = false` rethrows instead). Skip the dialog in CI with
`-Dnucleus.tao.fatalErrorDialog=false`.

To keep a window alive, provide `LocalWindowExceptionHandlerFactory` (`@ExperimentalComposeUiApi`):

```kotlin
CompositionLocalProvider(
    LocalWindowExceptionHandlerFactory provides WindowExceptionHandlerFactory { _ ->
        WindowExceptionHandler { throwable -> /* return to drop the frame, rethrow to exit */ }
    },
) {
    DecoratedWindow(onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication) { MyContent() }
}
```

A failure inside composition can't resume: close and recreate the window, or rethrow.

## Notes

- On a regular JVM, macOS needs `-XstartOnFirstThread`. The Nucleus plugin adds it to Hot Reload
  tasks. A native image doesn't need it.
- `NucleusApplicationScope` extends `ApplicationScope`, but composables that start AWT don't work.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- Each window composes in its own scene. Nucleus bridges the parent composition locals into it.
- The exception handler covers layout, draw, input, IME, accessibility, and `nativePopupLayers`
  popups, and runs on the thread where the failure happened.
- On Linux, input methods resolve like GTK widgets: ibus or fcitx5 on X11, text-input-v3 on
  Wayland. On macOS, the OS decides whether a held letter repeats or opens the accent picker.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## API reference

### DecoratedWindow parameters

| Parameter | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `onCloseRequest` | required | Close button, Alt+F4, Cmd+Q, and Dock > Quit. |
| `state` | `rememberWindowState()` | See [Window state](/docs/windows/window-state). |
| `visible` / `enabled` / `focusable` | `true` | |
| `title` / `icon` | `""` / `null` | |
| `resizable` / `minimizable` / `maximizable` | `true` | Reactive. |
| `alwaysOnTop` / `alwaysOnBottom` | `false` | Reactive. `alwaysOnBottom` clears `alwaysOnTop`. |
| `undecorated` | `false` | Borderless window with no controls. |
| `popupFor` | `null` | Linux: attach as a popup overlay of another window. |
| `nativePopupLayers` | `false` | See [Dialogs and popups](/docs/windows/dialogs-popups). |
| `nativeContextMenu` | `false` | See [Context menus](/docs/os/menus/context-menu). |
| `hiddenFromDock` | `false` | Hide from the taskbar or Dock. |
| `minimumSize` | `null` | The v2 overload uses `minSize` and `maxSize`. |
| `onPreviewKeyEvent` / `onKeyEvent` | `{ false }` | Return `true` to consume. |
| `transparent` / `forceX11` | `false` | Creation-time only. |
| `clickThrough` / `visibleOnAllWorkspaces` | `false` | Reactive. See [Overlay windows](/docs/windows/overlay-windows). |

### Title bar modifiers

- `Modifier.macOSLargeCornerRadius()`: macOS 26 large window corner radius.
- `Modifier.newFullscreenControls()`: layout for native fullscreen controls on macOS.

## What's next

- [Window state](/docs/windows/window-state): size, position, screens, and the window API v2.
- [Window scaffold and chrome](/docs/windows/window-scaffold): full-window layouts and materials.
- [Dialogs and popups](/docs/windows/dialogs-popups): modal dialogs and native popup surfaces.
- [Toolkits](/docs/toolkits): Material, Jewel, Fluent, Yaru, and macOS window themes.

# Window state

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/windows/window-state

Control and observe window size, position, placement, and screen with Compose's WindowState or the AWT-free window API v2 in dev.nucleusframework.window.tao.v2.

A state object sets and reports a window's size, position, placement, and screen. `DecoratedWindow`
accepts Compose's `WindowState` (v1, the default) and the window API v2 in
`dev.nucleusframework.window.tao.v2`, which also moves windows between screens.

## Use the v1 state

```kotlin
val state = rememberWindowState(
    size = DpSize(1100.dp, 720.dp),
    position = WindowPosition.Aligned(Alignment.Center),
)

DecoratedWindow(onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication, state = state) {
    Button(onClick = { state.placement = WindowPlacement.Maximized }) { Text("Maximize") }
}
```

`size`, `position`, `placement`, and `isMinimized` are mutable: write them to drive the window, read
them to follow the user. Dialogs take `rememberDialogState()` the same way.

## Size a window to its content

Set an axis to `Dp.Unspecified` and the window measures its content once, then takes that size:

```kotlin
val state = rememberWindowState(size = DpSize(Dp.Unspecified, Dp.Unspecified))
```

A dialog with a parent centres on it, and one without centres on the screen. Later content changes
don't resize the window.

## Use the window API v2

The v2 state replaces mutable properties with requests and adds screen selection:

```kotlin
import dev.nucleusframework.window.tao.v2.*

@OptIn(ExperimentalComposeUiApi::class)
fun main() = nucleusApplication {
    val state = rememberWindowState(
        initialScreenProvider = WindowScreenProvider.Primary,
        initialBoundsProvider = WindowBoundsProvider(
            sizeProvider = WindowSizeProvider.Fixed(1200.dp, 800.dp),
            positionProvider = WindowPositionProvider.CenteredOnScreen,
        ),
    )

    DecoratedWindow(onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication, state = state) {
        Button(onClick = { state.requestSize(900.dp, 600.dp) }) { Text("Resize") }
    }
}
```

The package mirrors Compose 1.12's `androidx.compose.ui.window.v2` member for member.
`DecoratedWindow`, `DecoratedDialog`, `HostedWindow`, and `HostedDialog` each have a v2 overload
that replaces `minimumSize` with `minSize` and `maxSize` (inner sizes). The `Decorated*` v2
overloads need `@OptIn(ExperimentalComposeUiApi::class)`.

Nucleus does not accept Compose's `androidx.compose.ui.window.v2` types: they depend on AWT. Change
the import to `dev.nucleusframework.window.tao.v2`. See [Migrate from 2.x](/docs/migrate/from-2.x).

## Request geometry changes

| Request | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `requestSize(...)` | Resize. |
| `requestPosition(...)` | Move. |
| `requestBounds(...)` | Resize and move together. |
| `requestPlacement(placement)` | `Floating`, `Maximized`, or `Fullscreen`. |
| `requestMinimized(value)` | Minimize or restore. |
| `requestScreen(provider)` | Move to another screen. |

Size, position, and bounds requests also take a provider. The window applies requests asynchronously: bounds requests in
order, and only the latest screen, placement, or minimized request. A bounds request restores a
maximized or fullscreen window first.

## Read the observed state

The window writes `bounds` (decorations included), `position`, `size`, `screenId`, `placement`, and
`isMinimized` back to the state. They throw until the window has been visible once:

```kotlin
val label = if (state.isInitialized) "${state.size} on ${state.screenId}" else "not shown yet"
```

`rememberSaveable` restores the last screen, placement, and bounds through `WindowState.Saver`.

## Move a window to another screen

```kotlin
state.requestScreen { screens.last() }
state.requestScreen(WindowScreenProvider.ById(savedScreenId))
```

The scope lists `screens`, `defaultScreen` (the current one), and `primaryScreen`. The window keeps
its relative position and stays fully visible. `ById` falls back to the default screen while that
display is unplugged. A `Screen` exposes `id`, `name`, `bounds`, `availableBounds` (minus taskbar,
menu bar, and docks), `insets`, and `isPrimary`, in dp.

To list displays outside a provider, call `TaoMonitors.all()`, `primary()`, `forWindow(taoWindow)`,
or `byId(id)` (`null` when unplugged). Their geometry is in physical pixels: convert with
`boundsDp(scale)` using the scale of the window you position.

## Size and place with providers

| `WindowSizeProvider` | Size |
| --- | --- |
| `Default` | 800 × 600 dp. |
| `Current` | Keeps the current size. |
| `Fixed(width, height)` | The given size. |
| `Unconstrained` | Content size, capped at the screen's available size. |
| `PreferredWidth(height)` / `PreferredHeight(width)` | Content size on one axis. |

| `WindowPositionProvider` | Position |
| --- | --- |
| `Default` | The window manager places the window. |
| `Current` | Keeps the current position. |
| `CenteredOnScreen` / `CenteredInParentWindow` | Centre of the screen or parent. |
| `Absolute(x, y)` | The given point. |
| `AlignedToScreen(alignment, offset)` | Aligned inside the available bounds. |
| `AlignedToParentWindow(anchor, alignment, offset, excludeParentInsets)` | Aligned around the parent. |

The parent-window providers throw when the window has no parent. `WindowBoundsProvider(size,
position)` combines the two. Prefer it over `WindowBoundsProvider.Absolute(rect)` when either side
is `Default` or content-sized: a `DpRect` can't express those.

A custom provider is a lambda with `windowMetrics`, `parentWindowMetrics`, `contentToWindowSize`, and
`measureWindowContent`:

```kotlin
state.requestBounds {
    val work = windowMetrics.screen.availableBounds
    DpRect(work.left, work.top, work.left + (work.right - work.left) / 2, work.bottom)
}
```

## Use a dialog state

`DialogState` has the screen and bounds requests of `WindowState`, without placement or minimize.
Create it with `rememberDialogState(initialScreenProvider, initialBoundsProvider)` or
`rememberDialogStateWithBounds(initialPosition, initialSize)`, which centres on the screen by
default. `rememberWindowStateWithBounds` is the window counterpart. See
[Dialogs and popups](/docs/windows/dialogs-popups).

## Known limits

- X11 window managers apply their own policy to the initial position. Openbox places it at 0,0.
- A themed `NucleusWindowHost` without the v2 overload drops `maxSize`. See
  [Route windows through a host](/docs/windows#route-windows-through-a-host).

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- The v2 package reads displays from `TaoMonitors` and geometry from the native window.
- `measureWindowContent` returns the current content size clamped to the constraints until the
  window exists, then runs a real measure pass.
- On macOS, Nucleus never toggles zoom to restore a window: setting the frame un-zooms it.
- When the platform names no primary monitor (GDK on Wayland), the first one takes `isPrimary`.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## What's next

- [Windows](/docs/windows): `DecoratedWindow` parameters and the window handle.
- [Dialogs and popups](/docs/windows/dialogs-popups): modal dialogs and their placement.
- [HiDPI](/docs/windows/hidpi): scale factors across monitors.
- [Multi-window apps](/docs/multi-window): satellites, docking, and tabs.

# Window scaffold and chrome

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/windows/window-scaffold

Build full-window layouts and custom title bars with WindowScaffold, drag areas, WindowControls, and the macOS and Windows 11 materials.

`WindowScaffold` lays out a custom title bar and the window content, and keeps the native caption
zones, button order and drag behavior working. It comes with `nucleus-application`. Use it when
content reaches under the title bar or a design system draws its own chrome; a plain
`DecoratedWindow` with `TitleBar` keeps working.

## Build a custom title bar

```kotlin
DecoratedWindow(onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication, title = "MyApp") {
    MaterialTheme {
        WindowBackground(MaterialTheme.colorScheme.background)
        WindowScaffold(
            titleBar = {
                Box(Modifier.fillMaxWidth().height(48.dp).windowDragArea().padding(horizontal = 12.dp)) {
                    Text("MyApp", Modifier.align(Alignment.CenterStart))
                    WindowControls(Modifier.align(Alignment.CenterEnd))
                }
            },
            titleBarPlacement = TitleBarPlacement.Overlay(),
        ) { contentPadding ->
            Box(Modifier.fillMaxSize().padding(contentPadding)) { /* content */ }
        }
    }
}
```

Make `WindowScaffold` the only child of the window content. It makes nothing draggable: mark the
move surface with `windowDragArea`.

## Place the title bar

| `TitleBarPlacement` | Layout |
| --- | --- |
| `Docked` | Default. The bar takes its height and the content fills the rest. |
| `Overlay(autoHideInFullscreen = true, passThroughToContent = false)` | The content fills the window, the bar floats on top, and the content gets the bar height as top padding. |

- `autoHideInFullscreen` removes the bar in fullscreen, and the chrome insets drop to zero.
- `passThroughToContent` also hit-tests presses on the bar against the content below. Turn it on
  for controls in the title-bar band, such as a tab strip. Leave it off when content scrolls behind
  an opaque bar.
- `controlButtonsDirection`: `Auto` follows the platform, `Rtl` moves the system buttons to the
  leading edge and flips the macOS traffic lights.

## Add drag areas

```kotlin
Modifier.windowDragArea(doubleClickAction = WindowDoubleClickAction.ToggleMaximize)
VerticalScrollbar(adapter, Modifier.noWindowDrag())
```

Buttons and text fields opt out on their own. Wrap scrollbars, sliders and resize handles in
`noWindowDrag()`. A double-click toggles maximize when the window is `resizable` and `maximizable`
or already maximized, except in fullscreen. `WindowDoubleClickAction.None` turns it off.

## Place the window controls

```kotlin
WindowControls(direction = ControlButtonsDirection.Auto, renderer = WindowControlsRenderer.Platform)
```

The buttons follow the window state and its `resizable`, `maximizable` and `minimizable` flags.
Close calls `onCloseRequest`. On Linux, `Auto` also follows the desktop's button layout. See
[Set the window chrome](/docs/windows#set-the-window-chrome).

`Platform` draws Fluent buttons on Windows and GNOME or KDE buttons on Linux. On macOS it draws
nothing and reserves the traffic-light space. To draw your own buttons, implement
`WindowControlsRenderer.Control(type, state, onClick)`.

## Match the window to the app theme

```kotlin
WindowBackground(MaterialTheme.colorScheme.background)
WindowAppearance(if (dark) WindowAppearanceMode.Dark else WindowAppearanceMode.Light)
val insets = LocalWindowChromeInsets.current
```

- `WindowBackground` shows during live resize and wherever Compose paints nothing. Without it, a
  dark app can flash white while the user resizes.
- `WindowAppearance` makes glass, traffic lights, menus and caption glyphs follow the app theme.
  `System` follows the OS. No effect on Linux.
- `insets.controlsInsets` is the space reserved for system controls and `titleBarHeight` the bar
  height. Both are zero outside a `WindowScaffold`. Pad with these insets or with `WindowControls`,
  not both.

## Add a macOS glass region

```kotlin
Modifier.windowGlassRegion(WindowGlassRegionKind.Sidebar, cornerRadius = 12.dp)
```

The region shows the wallpaper-tinted material of System Settings. Leave its background unpainted.
Kinds are `Sidebar`, `ContentList` and `Inspector` (macOS 14+, falls back to `ContentList`). There
is no full-window glass. No effect on other platforms.

## Add a Windows 11 backdrop

```kotlin
WindowsBackdrop(
    style = WindowsBackdropStyle.Mica, // Acrylic, MicaAlt, Default, None
    tint = Color.Unspecified,
    tier = WindowsBackdropTier.Auto,   // Modern, LegacyMica, Windows10Acrylic
)
```

The material shows wherever the app paints nothing, and `WindowBackground` is suspended meanwhile.
An unspecified `tint` leaves Mica untinted and gives Acrylic the window background at moderate
opacity. Older Windows versions degrade to the closest material. No effect on macOS and Linux.

Windows with a backdrop or `transparent = true` render grayscale text instead of ClearType.

## Make a transparent, borderless window

```kotlin
DecoratedWindow(onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication, undecorated = true, transparent = true) { /* ... */ }
```

`transparent` is a creation-time flag. Pixels left at alpha 0 show the desktop, and opaque
`WindowBackground` and title-bar clears become transparent. The Material and Jewel windows take the
same flag. For click-through windows, see [Overlay windows](/docs/windows/overlay-windows).

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- The scaffold sends the measured `titleBar` height to the native layer, which centres the macOS
  traffic lights and sizes the Windows caption zone.
- `windowDragArea()` reads `LocalTaoWindow`. Pass `window = taoWindow` when parent composition
  locals reach a child window's scene.
- The glass region is an `NSSplitViewController` pane under the Compose surface.
- Windows 11 before 22H2 maps both Mica styles to the single Mica attribute; Windows 10 falls back
  to acrylic when available.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## What's next

- [Windows](/docs/windows): `DecoratedWindow` parameters and the window chrome flags.
- [Toolkits](/docs/toolkits): prebuilt title bars for Material, Jewel, Fluent, Yaru, and macOS.
- [Accessibility](/docs/input/accessibility): Compose semantics exposed to VoiceOver, Narrator, and Orca.

# Dialogs and popups

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/windows/dialogs-popups

Open modal dialogs with DecoratedDialog, HostedDialog, or a toolkit dialog, and render Compose popups as native surfaces placed against the screen.

On this page, you'll open native dialogs owned by a window and turn Compose popups, menus and
tooltips into native surfaces that can leave the window.

## Open a dialog

Call `DecoratedDialog` from a window's content:

```kotlin
if (showSettings) {
    DecoratedDialog(
        onCloseRequest = { showSettings = false },
        state = rememberDialogState(size = DpSize(480.dp, 320.dp)),
        title = "Settings",
    ) {
        DialogTitleBar { _ -> Text("Settings") }
        SettingsContent()
    }
}
```

A dialog is not resizable by default and has no minimize or maximize button. The window that opens
it becomes its owner: the dialog stays above it, follows it across minimize, Spaces and workspaces,
stays out of the taskbar, and closes with it. The owner ignores pointer input while the dialog is
open but keeps its keyboard focus. A dialog declared at application scope blocks pointer input in
every window.

### Place the dialog

A dialog centres on its owner, or on the screen when it has none. Set `Dp.Unspecified` on an axis
of the size to fit the content ([Size a window to its content](/docs/windows/window-state#size-a-window-to-its-content)).
For screen selection and position providers, pass a v2 `DialogState` from
`dev.nucleusframework.window.tao.v2` ([Use a dialog state](/docs/windows/window-state#use-a-dialog-state)).

## Use a toolkit dialog

| Toolkit | Dialog | Title bar |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Material 3 | `dev.nucleusframework.window.material.MaterialDecoratedDialog` | `MaterialDialogTitleBar` |
| Material 2 | `dev.nucleusframework.window.material2.MaterialDecoratedDialog` | `MaterialDialogTitleBar` |
| Jewel | `dev.nucleusframework.window.jewel.JewelDecoratedDialog` | `JewelDialogTitleBar` |

The dialogs are extensions on `NucleusApplicationScope`. From a composable without a receiver:

```kotlin
with(LocalNucleusApplicationScope.current) {
    MaterialDecoratedDialog(onCloseRequest = onClose, title = "Confirm") {
        MaterialDialogTitleBar { _ -> Text("Confirm") }
        ConfirmContent(onClose)
    }
}
```

The receiver-less AWT overloads of `MaterialDecoratedDialog` and `JewelDecoratedDialog` are gone,
and the Material 2 dialog is now a `NucleusApplicationScope` extension. See
[Migrate from 2.x](/docs/migrate/from-2.x).

- To let an app choose the dialog chrome for a library, call `HostedDialog`. See
  [Route windows through a host](/docs/windows#route-windows-through-a-host).
- Compose Desktop's AWT `DialogWindow` is unsupported. Compose's in-window `Dialog`, which
  `AlertDialog` uses, works in any Nucleus window.

## Open popups as native surfaces

By default the window edge clips a `Popup`, `DropdownMenu` or tooltip. With
`nativePopupLayers = true`, each popup of the window opens in its own native surface:

```kotlin
DecoratedWindow(onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication, nativePopupLayers = true) { /* ... */ }
```

`HostedWindow`, `MaterialDecoratedWindow` and `JewelDecoratedWindow` take the same parameter. Jewel's
`ListComboBox`, `PopupMenu`, `Dropdown` and tooltips go through it too.

### How popups meet the screen

- Inside a popup, `LocalWindowInfo` reports the display's work area, not the owner window. Position
  providers flip against the screen edge, and a tall menu in a small window gets its full height.
- The popup stays inside the work area of its display and follows the owner across monitors.
- A Compose `Dialog` (with a scrim) keeps the owner window's size and does not follow the display.

## Opt in a single subtree

`NativePopupLayers { }` gives native surfaces to the popups opened directly inside it:

```kotlin
NativePopupLayers {
    DropdownMenu(expanded = expanded, onDismissRequest = { expanded = false }) { /* ... */ }
}
```

Submenus opened from a native surface need no opt-in. `NativePopupLayers` does nothing when the
window already sets `nativePopupLayers = true`, when native popups are unavailable, or outside a
Nucleus window. The native [context menu](/docs/os/menus/context-menu) flyout on Windows and Linux
always uses it.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- Popup surfaces: an `NSPanel` child window on macOS, a transparent `WS_POPUP` HWND on Windows, an
  override-redirect window on X11 and a `wl_subsurface` on Wayland. On Windows and Linux the popup
  is re-clamped on every owner move.
- The surface extends 32 dp past the popup bounds so shadows and slide-in animations are not clipped.
- `DialogTitleBar` draws the close button only where the platform needs Compose-drawn chrome.
- A `LocalWindowExceptionHandlerFactory` also covers the popups of its window.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## What's next

- [Context menus](/docs/os/menus/context-menu): the platform menu and the Fluent and Adwaita flyouts.
- [Window state](/docs/windows/window-state): dialog size, position, and screen.
- [Overlay windows](/docs/windows/overlay-windows): transparent, click-through, and always-on-bottom windows.

# Overlay windows

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/windows/overlay-windows

Build watermarks, desktop widgets, and heads-up overlays with transparent, click-through, always-on-bottom, and all-workspaces windows.

An overlay sits outside the normal window stack: a watermark that ignores clicks, a widget pinned
below other windows, a badge that follows you across workspaces. You build one with
`DecoratedWindow` flags from `nucleus-application`.

## Build a click-through watermark

```kotlin
fun main(args: Array<String>) = nucleusApplication(args) {
    DecoratedWindow(
        onCloseRequest = { },
        state = rememberWindowState(
            position = WindowPosition.Aligned(Alignment.BottomEnd),
            size = DpSize(360.dp, 160.dp),
        ),
        title = "Watermark",
        resizable = false,
        undecorated = true,
        transparent = true,
        alwaysOnTop = true,
        focusable = false,
        clickThrough = true,
        hiddenFromDock = true,
        visibleOnAllWorkspaces = true,
        forceX11 = true,
    ) {
        Watermark()
    }
}
```

Pair `clickThrough = true` with `focusable = false`: a window you cannot click has no use for
keyboard focus.

## Pin a widget below other windows

A desktop widget swaps `alwaysOnTop` for `alwaysOnBottom` and keeps clicks:

```kotlin
DecoratedWindow(
    onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication,
    title = "Nucleus widget",
    undecorated = true,
    transparent = true,
    hiddenFromDock = true,
    nativeContextMenu = true,
    visibleOnAllWorkspaces = true,
    forceX11 = true,
    alwaysOnBottom = true,
) {
    WidgetSurface()
}
```

`alwaysOnTop` and `alwaysOnBottom` exclude each other: the last one you set wins.

The window still shows in the taskbar and Alt+Tab unless you set `hiddenFromDock`. Native Wayland
cannot glue a surface to the wallpaper.

## Toggle flags at run time

`clickThrough`, `alwaysOnBottom`, and `visibleOnAllWorkspaces` are reactive. For imperative
control, call the setters on `nucleusWindow.unsafe.taoWindow`:

```kotlin
fun applyOverlayMode(window: TaoWindow, passive: Boolean) {
    window.setIgnoreCursorEvents(passive)
    window.setAlwaysOnBottom(passive)
    window.setVisibleOnAllWorkspaces(passive)
}
```

`transparent` and `forceX11` apply at creation only.

## Take an X11 surface on Wayland

Stacking, position, and workspace flags do nothing on a native Wayland surface. `forceX11 = true`
gives one window an XWayland surface and leaves the rest of the app on Wayland. To move the whole
process, set `NUCLEUS_TAO_LINUX_RENDERER=x11` (or `GDK_BACKEND=x11`) before launch.

`TaoWindow.isNativeWaylandSurface` tells you which surface a window received, after it is ready.
To decide whether you can position a window, branch on `canPlaceOnScreen` instead. See
[Linux and Wayland](/docs/windows/linux-wayland#branch-on-screen-placement).

If `forceX11` finds no X server, the window stays on Wayland. Nucleus logs a warning for each flag
that a native Wayland surface ignores.

## Platform behavior

**macOS**

A transparent window keeps a shadow shaped to the drawn content. Floating above another app's
full-screen Space is not supported.

**Windows**

`visibleOnAllWorkspaces` is a no-op. A window with `hiddenFromDock = true` already shows on every
virtual desktop. A fully transparent window drops the system shadow and border.

**Linux**

Transparency works on X11 and Wayland. `alwaysOnBottom`, `visibleOnAllWorkspaces`, and positioning
need X11: use `forceX11` per window or `NUCLEUS_TAO_LINUX_RENDERER=x11` for the process.

A mostly transparent window reads better with `undecorated = true` and custom chrome than with the
stock `TitleBar`.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- macOS: `clickThrough` sets `NSWindow.ignoresMouseEvents`, `visibleOnAllWorkspaces` uses
  `NSWindowCollectionBehaviorCanJoinAllSpaces`.
- Windows: `clickThrough` applies `WS_EX_TRANSPARENT | WS_EX_LAYERED`, `alwaysOnBottom` uses
  `HWND_BOTTOM`.
- Linux: `clickThrough` installs an empty GDK input region, `alwaysOnBottom` maps to
  `_NET_WM_STATE_BELOW`, `visibleOnAllWorkspaces` to `gtk_window_stick()`.
- Nucleus marks the Compose scene transparent, so dialog scrims and popups blend against the alpha
  background.
- Native Wayland ignores `WindowPosition.Aligned`; Nucleus logs this once per process.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## API reference

| Parameter | Default | Reactive | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `transparent` | `false` | No | Native surface with an alpha channel. |
| `clickThrough` | `false` | Yes | Pointer events pass to whatever sits behind. |
| `alwaysOnBottom` | `false` | Yes | Keeps the window below normal windows. Clears `alwaysOnTop`. |
| `visibleOnAllWorkspaces` | `false` | Yes | Shows the window on every workspace or Space. |
| `forceX11` | `false` | No | Linux only: XWayland surface for this window. |

`HostedWindow` takes `alwaysOnBottom`. The Material and Jewel wrappers take `transparent`,
`clickThrough`, `visibleOnAllWorkspaces`, and `forceX11`.

| `TaoWindow` member | Description |
|---|---|
| `setIgnoreCursorEvents(ignore)` | Imperative `clickThrough`. |
| `setAlwaysOnBottom(alwaysOnBottom)` | Imperative `alwaysOnBottom`. |
| `setVisibleOnAllWorkspaces(visible)` | Imperative `visibleOnAllWorkspaces`. |
| `isNativeWaylandSurface` | Window runs on a native Wayland surface. |
| `canPlaceOnScreen` | App can read and set the window's screen position. |

## What's next

- [Windows](/docs/windows): the other `DecoratedWindow` parameters.
- [Linux and Wayland](/docs/windows/linux-wayland): session detection, screen placement, and the
  X11 fallback.
- [Context menus](/docs/os/menus/context-menu): the menu an interactive widget needs.

# Linux and Wayland

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/windows/linux-wayland

How Nucleus windows run on native Wayland and X11, what the compositor controls, and how to branch on screen placement.

On Linux, Nucleus windows run as native Wayland surfaces in a Wayland session and as X11 windows
elsewhere, with no code change and no dependency beyond `nucleus-application`. On native Wayland
the compositor owns window positions.

## Detect the session

Read the session type for diagnostics, or to gate features that differ per session, such as
taskbar progress and global hotkeys:

```kotlin
val onWayland = Platform.isWayland
val desktopEnv = if (Platform.Current == Platform.Linux) LinuxDesktopEnvironment.Current else null
```

`Platform.isWayland` describes the session, not a window: a window opened with `forceX11` runs on
XWayland inside a Wayland session. For a per-window answer, read
`TaoWindow.isNativeWaylandSurface` once the window is ready.

## Branch on screen placement

On native Wayland, the app can neither read nor set a window's screen position. Check
`TaoWindow.canPlaceOnScreen` before you read a window origin, move a window, or place one window
against another:

```kotlin
fun savedPosition(window: TaoWindow): IntOffset? {
    // Native Wayland: the compositor owns placement, so the origin is meaningless
    if (!window.canPlaceOnScreen) return null
    val (x, y) = window.outerBoundsPx() ?: return null
    return IntOffset(x.toInt(), y.toInt())
}
```

`canPlaceOnScreen` is `false` only on a native Wayland surface. The size from `outerBoundsPx()`
stays valid everywhere. Branch on this property, not on the compositor name or
`LinuxDesktopEnvironment`.

Where it is `false`:

- `WindowPosition` and `WindowPosition.Aligned` have no effect. Persist the window size, not its
  position.
- Start window moves from a `Modifier.windowDragArea` region.
- In cross-window drags (tearing off a tab, docking a satellite), a snapshot follows the pointer
  instead of the window. See [Multi-window](/docs/multi-window). Satellite chrome reads the same
  answer through `SatelliteScope.isCompositorPlaced`, see
  [Floating satellites on Wayland](/docs/multi-window/satellites#floating-satellites-on-wayland).

## Run on XWayland

Set `NUCLEUS_TAO_LINUX_RENDERER=x11` (or `GDK_BACKEND=x11`) before launch to put the whole process
on XWayland, where every window can read and set its position:

```shell
NUCLEUS_TAO_LINUX_RENDERER=x11 ./gradlew run
```

To move a single window, pass `forceX11 = true` to it. See
[Overlay windows](/docs/windows/overlay-windows#take-an-x11-surface-on-wayland).

## Wayland and X11 differences

| Concern | Native Wayland | X11 / XWayland |
|---|---|---|
| Window position | Compositor decides, reported as `(0, 0)` | Read and set |
| `alwaysOnTop`, `alwaysOnBottom` | No effect | Supported |
| Workspace stickiness | No effect | Supported |
| `hiddenFromDock` | No effect | Supported |
| Trackpad pinch | Delivered | Not delivered |
| Fractional scaling | Integer render, compositor scales | Integer scale |

## Copy and paste

Use the standard Compose `LocalClipboard` API. Plain text, images and file lists work in both
directions, and pasted files land in file managers. HTML does not cross, and Nucleus ignores the
X11 PRIMARY (middle-click) selection.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- The `xdg-shell` protocol exposes no window position, so GDK reports every native toplevel at
  `(0, 0)` and ignores moves. Nucleus logs `WindowPosition` being ignored once per process.
- When code asks native Wayland for stacking, positioning, stickiness or a screen-space drag,
  Nucleus logs a `java.util.logging` warning that suggests `NUCLEUS_TAO_LINUX_RENDERER=x11`.
- GDK's Wayland backend names no primary monitor, so `TaoMonitors.all()` flags the first one.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## API reference

| Symbol | Description |
|---|---|
| `TaoWindow.canPlaceOnScreen` | `false` on a native Wayland surface, where the app can neither read nor set the window position. |
| `TaoWindow.isNativeWaylandSurface` | Whether this window runs on a native Wayland surface. Read after the window is ready. |
| `TaoWindow.outerBoundsPx()` | `[x, y, width, height]` in physical pixels, or `null` before the window exists. |
| `Platform.isWayland` | `true` in a Linux session where `XDG_SESSION_TYPE` is `wayland` or `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` is set. |
| `LinuxDesktopEnvironment.Current` | `Gnome`, `KDE`, `XFCE`, `Cinnamon`, `Mate`, or `Unknown`. |
| `NUCLEUS_TAO_LINUX_RENDERER=x11` | Environment variable that puts the process on XWayland. |

Inside window content, reach the `TaoWindow` with `nucleusWindow.unsafe.taoWindow`.

## What's next

- [Multi-window](/docs/multi-window): satellites, docking, and tabs, and how they drag on Wayland.
- [Overlay windows](/docs/windows/overlay-windows): `forceX11` and the flags Wayland ignores.
- [HiDPI and text rendering](/docs/windows/hidpi): how scale factors map to Compose density.

# HiDPI and text rendering

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/windows/hidpi

How Nucleus windows follow each monitor's scale factor, and how ClearType text works on Windows.

Every Nucleus window tracks the scale factor of the display it sits on and re-renders when that
factor changes. Keep your layout in `Dp`: `Modifier.size(48.dp)` covers 48 device pixels at 1.0
and 96 at 2.0.

## Read the current density

```kotlin
@Composable
fun ShowDensity() {
    val density = LocalDensity.current
    Text("Scale: ${density.density}x · font scale: ${density.fontScale}")
}
```

`LocalDensity` updates when you move the window to another display, plug in a monitor, or change
the system scale. Outside composition, read `TaoWindow.scaleFactor`, or each display's
`TaoMonitor.scaleFactor`:

```kotlin
val scales = TaoMonitors.all().associate { it.name to it.scaleFactor }
```

On Linux, scale factors are integers. On a fractional Wayland output (125 %, 150 %), Nucleus
renders at the integer scale and the compositor scales the result.

## Render ClearType text on Windows

Opaque windows on Windows now draw text with LCD (ClearType) antialiasing instead of grayscale.
See [Migrate from 2.x](/docs/migrate/from-2.x).

You write no code for it. It works under HotSpot, ProGuard and GraalVM Native Image, and needs the
Nucleus Gradle plugin's `nucleus.application { }` setup. Text stays grayscale on popups,
`NativeView` overlays, Mica and Acrylic backdrops, `transparent = true` windows, and when ClearType
is off in Windows.

### Turn LCD text off

Keep grayscale text at run time:

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
nucleus.application {
    jvmArgs("-Dnucleus.text.lcd=false")
}
```

Or skip the build-time patch, which also makes the runtime property a no-op:

```properties title="gradle.properties"
nucleus.text.lcd.patch=false
```

## Notes

- Hold window sizes in `Dp`, never in pixels, so they survive a scale change.
- On Windows, popups and `DecoratedDialog` take the DPI and work area of the monitor they open on,
  even when it differs from the owner's.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- Windows declares Per-Monitor V2 DPI awareness at startup, also in GraalVM native images.
- The Gradle plugin patches `FontRasterizationSettings.PlatformDefault` in `ui-text-desktop` and
  fails the build if the patched Compose classes change shape.
- On Linux, `nucleusApplication` calls `applyLinuxHiDpiScale()` at startup for AWT and Swing code.
  Unless `sun.java2d.uiScale` is already set, it sets it and sets `GDK_SCALE` when the session has
  not. Nucleus windows do not depend on it.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## API reference

| Symbol | Description |
|---|---|
| `LocalDensity.current` | Compose density of the window the composable renders in. |
| `TaoWindow.scaleFactor` | Current scale factor of the window's monitor. |
| `TaoMonitors.all()` / `TaoMonitor.scaleFactor` | Every attached display and its scale factor. |
| `-Dnucleus.text.lcd=false` | Runtime: keep grayscale text on Windows. |
| `-Pnucleus.text.lcd.patch=false` | Build: skip the LCD patch of `ui-text-desktop`. |

## What's next

- [Windows](/docs/windows): the window you render your UI into.
- [Window state](/docs/windows/window-state): sizes, screens, and placement.
- [Linux and Wayland](/docs/windows/linux-wayland): session detection and Wayland behavior.

# Multi-window

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/multi-window

The two multi-window archetypes of Nucleus, satellite palettes that dock and Chrome-like tabs, and the workspace model they share.

Nucleus ships two multi-window archetypes, declared from `nucleusApplication` and included in
`nucleus-application`: satellite palettes that float beside a document or dock into it, and
Chrome-like tabs that tear off into windows of their own.

Every API in this section is `@ExperimentalNucleusApi` at level `ERROR`. Add
`@OptIn(ExperimentalNucleusApi::class)`, or opt the module in with
`optIn.add("dev.nucleusframework.window.ExperimentalNucleusApi")` in `kotlin.compilerOptions`.

## Pick an archetype

| | Satellites | Tabs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What the user sees | Tool palettes, inspectors, panes around a document | Documents as tabs in a strip at the top of each window |
| Who opens windows | You open the document windows; palettes follow the focused one | The workspace: one window per group of tabs |
| Moves | Float ↔ dock, dock ↔ dock, between document windows | Reorder, tear off, merge into another window |
| Declaration | `Satellite(workspace, id, title) { … }` | `Tab(workspace, id, title) { … }` |
| Page | [Satellites](/docs/multi-window/satellites), [Docking](/docs/multi-window/docking) | [Tabs](/docs/multi-window/tabs) |

The two compose: a tab window can host its own `DockLayout`. See
[Compose tabs with satellites](/docs/multi-window/tabs#compose-tabs-with-satellites).
`Satellite`, `SatelliteWindow`, `Tab` and `TabWindows` live in `dev.nucleusframework.application`,
the rest in `dev.nucleusframework.window.tao`.

## Shared ideas

- **The workspace owns placement.** Declare each satellite or tab once, at application scope. The
  workspace picks the host window and moves it on drag. `initialPlacement`, `initiallyOpen` and
  `group` apply on the first declaration of an `id` only.
- **Entries outlive composition.** A satellite or tab declared again resumes where it was.
  `snapshot()` and `restore()` persist the layout.
- **State follows the content.** `rememberSaveable` survives every move between windows. Plain
  `remember` does not: hoist it or make it saveable.

### Two ways to carry a drag

`SatelliteWorkspace.dragKind` and `TabWorkspace.dragKind` hold the `WorkspaceDragKind` of the drag
in flight, or `null`.

| Value | When | What follows the pointer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Window` | Windows, macOS, X11, XWayland | A real window, or a ghost window |
| `Transfer` | `TaoWindow.canPlaceOnScreen == false` (native Wayland) | The compositor's drag icon; `dragGhost` stays `null` |

Branch Wayland-sensitive chrome on `TaoWindow.canPlaceOnScreen`, or
`SatelliteScope.isCompositorPlaced`, never on the compositor name.
`NUCLEUS_TAO_LINUX_RENDERER=x11` runs the app on XWayland and restores window-following drags.

## Run the demos

Run one with `./gradlew :examples:<name>:run`.

| Demo | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| [`satellite-demo`](https://github.com/NucleusFramework/Nucleus/tree/main/examples/satellite-demo) | Shared palettes, owner follows focus or a pin, drag to dock, layout snapshots |
| [`tabs-demo`](https://github.com/NucleusFramework/Nucleus/tree/main/examples/tabs-demo) | Tear-off, merge, reorder, hover cards with thumbnails |
| [`jewel-tabs-demo`](https://github.com/NucleusFramework/Nucleus/tree/main/examples/jewel-tabs-demo) | The tab workspace drawn with Jewel's `TabStrip` |
| [`tab-satellites-demo`](https://github.com/NucleusFramework/Nucleus/tree/main/examples/tab-satellites-demo) | One `SatelliteWorkspace` per tab window |
| [`reader-dock-demo`](https://github.com/NucleusFramework/Nucleus/tree/main/examples/reader-dock-demo) | Right-to-left reader: layered sides, custom splitters and headers, fixed panes |

## What's next

- [Satellites](/docs/multi-window/satellites): declare palettes and let them follow the focused document.
- [Docking](/docs/multi-window/docking): lay docked panels out around your content.
- [Tabs](/docs/multi-window/tabs): turn documents into tabs that tear off into windows.
- [Linux and Wayland](/docs/windows/linux-wayland): what a compositor-placed window changes.

# Satellites

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/multi-window/satellites

Declare tool palettes and inspectors once, let them follow the focused document window, dock them, and save the layout.

A satellite is a native window that belongs to another window: it follows its parent, stays
above it, hides with it, and keeps out of the taskbar. The user can float it or dock it into the
document. Satellites are `@ExperimentalNucleusApi` (see [Multi-window](/docs/multi-window)).

## Declare a workspace

Document windows join a `SatelliteWorkspace` with `JoinSatelliteWorkspace`. Declare satellites at
application scope, next to the windows:

```kotlin title="Main.kt"
fun main() = nucleusApplication {
    val workspace = rememberSatelliteWorkspace()

    DecoratedWindow(onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication, title = "Document") {
        JoinSatelliteWorkspace(workspace)
        WindowScaffold(titleBar = { TitleBar { Text("Document") } }) { padding ->
            DockLayout(workspace, Modifier.padding(padding)) { Document() }
        }
    }

    Satellite(workspace, id = "tools", title = "Tools") { ToolsPanel() }
    Satellite(
        workspace,
        id = "colors",
        title = "Colors",
        initialPlacement = SatellitePlacement.Docked(DockSide.Right),
    ) { ColorPanel() }
}
```

`Tools` opens as a floating window, `Colors` as a docked panel. Each gets a header with Dock,
Float and Close actions; dragging it moves the satellite between the two hosts.

## Satellite parameters

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `workspace`, `id`, `title` | required | Workspace, stable identity, header and window title |
| `initialPlacement` | `SatellitePlacement.Floating()` | Where it starts on first declaration |
| `initiallyOpen` | `true` | Whether it is shown on first declaration |
| `dockSides` | all four `DockSide`s | Sides it may dock on. Empty makes a floating-only palette |
| `floatable` | `true` | `false` makes a fixed panel. Requires a docked `initialPlacement` |
| `reorderable` | `true` | `false` pins its rank on its side. Requires a docked `initialPlacement` |
| `resizable` | `true` | Whether the user can resize the floating window |
| `hideWhileOwnerFullscreenOrMaximized` | `true` | Hide the floating window while the owner fills the screen |
| `nativeContextMenu` | `true` | Native context menu for text fields in the floating window |
| `header` | `{ DefaultSatelliteHeader() }` | Chrome in the floating title bar and above the docked panel |
| `floatingCaption` | `{}` | See [Floating satellites on Wayland](#floating-satellites-on-wayland) |
| `content` | required | The body, with `SatelliteScope` as receiver |

`initialPlacement` through `reorderable` apply the first time an `id` is declared, unless `restore`
placed it. Contradicting values throw. Docking options are on [Docking](/docs/multi-window/docking).

## Choose where a satellite starts

`SatellitePlacement.Docked(side, order = 0, extent = null, weight = 1f)` puts it in the owner's
`DockLayout`. See [Size a docked panel](/docs/multi-window/docking#size-a-docked-panel).
`SatellitePlacement.Floating` places a window relative to the owner:

```kotlin
SatellitePlacement.Floating(
    positioner = WindowPositioner(
        parentAnchor = WindowAnchor.Right,
        childAnchor = WindowAnchor.Left,
        offset = DpOffset(12.dp, 0.dp),
        constraintAdjustment = WindowConstraintAdjustment.FlipAndSlide,
    ),
    size = DpSize(300.dp, 400.dp), // default 320 × 240 dp
)
```

The default positioner puts it at the owner's top-right corner with a 12 dp gap. `anchorRect`
anchors to a rectangle of the owner instead of its frame. `constraintAdjustment` keeps the window
on the monitor: `None`, `Slide`, `Flip`, `FlipAndSlide` (default) or `All` (also shrinks).

Placement runs once. To apply a new rule later, set `entry.windowState.positioner` and call
`entry.windowState.reanchor()`.

## Choose the owner

Floating satellites follow the workspace's `owner`: the member focused last with
`followFocus = true` (the default), else the pinned member or the first to join.
`workspace.pinTo(window)` forces an owner; `pinTo(null)` undoes it.

## Drive satellites from code

| Call | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `open(id)` / `close(id)` / `toggle(id)` | Show or hide; placement and state are kept |
| `dock(id, side, order = null, host = null)` | Dock on `side` of `host`, else the current dock host, else the owner |
| `undock(id, placement = null)` | Float it over its panel, or at `placement` |
| `visible` | `false` hides every satellite without closing any |
| `owner`, `pinnedOwner`, `members`, `satellites`, `satellite(id)` | Snapshot state to read |

Call the workspace from effects and UI callbacks, not during composition.

## Write a header

`header` and `content` run with `SatelliteScope`: `workspace`, `satellite` (the entry),
`isDocked`, `isCompositorPlaced`, and `dock(side)`, `undock()`, `close()`.

A custom header puts `Modifier.satelliteDragHandle(scope)` on the docked strip only. The floating
title bar already carries the handle, and a second one would start two drags. A press without
movement does nothing, so buttons can sit inside the handle.

```kotlin
@Composable
fun SatelliteScope.PaneHeader() {
    Row(
        Modifier
            .fillMaxWidth()
            .height(32.dp)
            .then(if (isDocked) Modifier.satelliteDragHandle(this) else Modifier),
        verticalAlignment = Alignment.CenterVertically,
    ) {
        Text(satellite.title, Modifier.weight(1f))
        if (isDocked) {
            if (satellite.isFloatable) IconButton(onClick = { undock() }) { Text("↗") }
        } else {
            IconButton(onClick = { dock() }) { Text("↙") }
        }
        IconButton(onClick = { close() }) { Text("—") }
    }
}
```

## Save and restore the layout

```kotlin
val saved = workspace.snapshot()   // SatelliteLayoutSnapshot
workspace.restore(saved)
```

`SatelliteLayoutSnapshot` holds each satellite's `placement` and `isOpen`, plus the side
extents. It is a plain data class; you serialize it. `restore` also applies to satellites
declared later and leaves unnamed ones alone.

## Floating satellites on Wayland

On a compositor-placed window only the compositor can move the window. The floating title bar
splits there: the header docks the satellite, and a 56 dp strip (`SatelliteCaptionStripWidth`)
beside the window controls moves the window. Nucleus composes `floatingCaption` in that strip,
only when `isCompositorPlaced` is `true`. Put a "move" glyph there, not a control.

## Open a standalone satellite window

`SatelliteWindow` attaches one palette to one window, without a workspace or docking:

```kotlin
DecoratedWindow(onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication) {
    var inspector by remember { mutableStateOf(true) }
    if (inspector) {
        SatelliteWindow(
            onCloseRequest = { inspector = false },
            state = rememberSatelliteWindowState(
                size = DpSize(260.dp, 420.dp),
                positioner = WindowPositioner(WindowAnchor.TopRight, WindowAnchor.TopLeft),
            ),
            title = "Inspector",
        ) { InspectorPanel() }
    }
}
```

`onCloseRequest` also fires when the parent is destroyed. `parent` defaults to the enclosing
window, and the default positioner centers the satellite on it. The other parameters match
`DecoratedWindow`, plus `hideWhileParentFullscreenOrMaximized` and `nativeContextMenu`. The state
publishes `offsetFromParent` (`null` on native Wayland), `isHiddenByParent` and `isActive`.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- A satellite keeps its offset from the parent's top-left corner, including one the user set by
  dragging. Its position is resolved before the window is shown, so it never flashes elsewhere.
- When a focused satellite closes or docks, Nucleus focuses its parent, so Windows does not
  activate another application's window.
- Satellite windows cannot maximize, which would break anchoring and the dock hit-test.
- On native Wayland the compositor places a `SatelliteWindow` and it does not follow the parent.
- On Windows the positioner uses the parent's monitor; macOS and Linux use the primary monitor.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## What's next

- [Docking](/docs/multi-window/docking): side order, split and layered sides, fixed panels.
- [Tabs](/docs/multi-window/tabs): give each tab window its own satellites.
- [Linux and Wayland](/docs/windows/linux-wayland): compositor-placed windows.
