# Docking

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/multi-window/docking

Lay docked satellites out around your content with DockLayout, size and order the panels, restrict where they go, and draw your own splitters.

`DockLayout` lays the satellites docked into a window around that window's content. It is
`@ExperimentalNucleusApi` (see [Multi-window](/docs/multi-window)).

## Add a dock layout

Compose `DockLayout` inside a window that joined the workspace:

```kotlin
DecoratedWindow(onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication) {
    JoinSatelliteWorkspace(workspace)
    WindowScaffold(titleBar = { TitleBar { Text("Document") } }) { padding ->
        DockLayout(
            workspace,
            Modifier.fillMaxSize().padding(padding),
            sideOrder = listOf(DockSide.Right, DockSide.Bottom, DockSide.Left, DockSide.Top),
            layeredSides = setOf(DockSide.Right),
        ) { Document() }
    }
}
```

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `workspace` | required | The `SatelliteWorkspace` whose panels it hosts |
| `host` | `LocalTaoWindow.current` | The window `SatelliteEntry.dockHost` refers to |
| `sideOrder` | `DefaultDockSideOrder` | The four sides, outermost first |
| `layeredSides` | `emptySet()` | Sides whose panels are layers instead of a split |
| `splitter` | `{ DefaultDockSplitter() }` | Drawn between a side and the content, and between two panels |
| `panel` | `{ it() }` | Frame around each panel (`SatelliteScope` receiver); must invoke the lambda |
| `content` | required | The document |

The outermost side runs the full length of the layout and owns its corners. Name each `DockSide`
once. `DefaultDockSideOrder` is `listOf(Top, Bottom, Left, Right)`, which differs from
`DockSide.entries`.

## Choose split or layered sides

| | Split (default) | Layered (`layeredSides`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Arrangement | Panels divide the side's length | Each panel is a full-length layer, from the edge inwards |
| Thickness | Shared: `workspace.dockExtent(side)` | Per panel: `Docked.extent` |
| Length | By `Docked.weight` | Full length |

A layered side with three panels gives three columns, each with its own width and splitter.

## Size a docked panel

`SatellitePlacement.Docked(side, order = 0, extent = null, weight = 1f)` carries the geometry.
`extent` applies on a layered side (`null` uses the side's `dockExtent`); `weight` applies on a
split side and must be positive. The splitters update both, and snapshots store them.

| Workspace call | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `dockExtent(side)` / `setDockExtent(side, extent)` | Shared thickness of a split side; 280 dp until set |
| `setDockedExtent(id, extent)` | A panel's own `extent`, clamped to its limits |
| `setDockedWeight(id, weight)` | A panel's `weight` |
| `plannedDockExtent(entry, side)` | The thickness `side` would have once `entry` docks there |

A docked palette keeps the width it had as a floating window. When the window is too small, the
panels shrink proportionally and get their stored extents back when it grows.

### Bound the thickness

A satellite has a `minExtent` (at least 80 dp) and a `maxExtent` (unbounded). Docking, splitters
and `restore()` respect them; the floating window ignores them. Only the `Satellite` overload in
`dev.nucleusframework.window.tao` (receiver `taoApplication`) takes them in this release; the
`nucleusApplication` overload uses the defaults.

## Draw splitters

The `splitter` slot runs with `DockSplitterScope`: `side`, `orientation` (`Horizontal` for a
vertical line), and `panel` (the panel it resizes, `null` for a split side's `dockExtent`).
Apply `Modifier.dockSplitterHandle()` to the element the user grabs, which can be wider than
what you draw:

```kotlin
@Composable
fun DockSplitterScope.ThinSplitter() {
    val horizontal = orientation == Orientation.Horizontal
    val line = if (horizontal) Modifier.fillMaxHeight().width(1.dp) else Modifier.fillMaxWidth().height(1.dp)
    Box(line.background(MaterialTheme.colorScheme.outlineVariant), contentAlignment = Alignment.Center) {
        val grip = if (horizontal) Modifier.requiredWidth(5.dp).fillMaxHeight() else Modifier.requiredHeight(5.dp).fillMaxWidth()
        Box(grip.dockSplitterHandle())
    }
}
```

## Restrict where a panel goes

The workspace enforces these `Satellite` parameters in drags, `dock()`, `undock()`, `restore()`
and the default header.

| Parameter | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `dockSides` | all four | Only these sides are offered. Empty: a floating-only palette |
| `floatable` | `true` | `false` is a fixed panel that never becomes a window |
| `reorderable` | `true` | `false` pins its rank; nothing can be dropped in front of it |

`floatable = false` and `reorderable = false` require a docked `initialPlacement`.

## Rank panels

`Docked.order` counts from the top or left on a split side, and from the edge on a layered side.
`dock(id, side, order)` inserts at `order`; without `order`, the panel returns to its last rank
on that side, else the end. Pinned panels keep their declared rank.

## Draw your own drop feedback

During a drag, each `DockLayout` lights the zones it accepts and previews the space a release
would fill. For custom feedback read `workspace.dockPreview` (a `DockTarget(host, side, order)`),
`draggedSatellite` and `dragGhost`, which is `null` on native Wayland. See
[Two ways to carry a drag](/docs/multi-window#two-ways-to-carry-a-drag).

`DockSide` values are physical, also in right-to-left apps: put RTL navigation on
`DockSide.Right`.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- Panels and content are `movableContentOf`: no layout change rebuilds a subtree. Only leaving
  the host window disposes a panel.
- On a split side, the thickest minimum and the thinnest maximum win; the minimum wins if they
  cross.
- Each allowed edge has a 64 dp drop zone (`SatelliteWorkspace.DockZoneWidth`). Where windows
  overlap, the owner's layout is tried first, then the others by focus recency.
- The layout runs left-to-right internally so splitters drag the right way, then restores your
  `LayoutDirection` for the content.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## What's next

- [Satellites](/docs/multi-window/satellites): declare palettes, headers and layouts.
- [Tabs](/docs/multi-window/tabs#compose-tabs-with-satellites): hang one dock per tab window.
- [Pointer icons](/docs/input/pointer-icons): the grab and resize cursors the handles use.

# Tabs

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/multi-window/tabs

Declare documents as Chrome-like tabs that reorder, tear off into windows and merge back, with custom strips, previews and saved layouts.

`TabWindows` and `Tab` give an app the Chrome tab model: a tab strip in every window's title bar,
windows that appear when a tab is torn off and close when their last tab leaves. Tabs are
`@ExperimentalNucleusApi` (see [Multi-window](/docs/multi-window)).

## Declare tabs

Create a `TabWorkspace`, compose `TabWindows` once, and declare every tab at application scope:

```kotlin title="Main.kt"
fun main() = nucleusApplication {
    val workspace = rememberTabWorkspace()
    TabWindows(workspace, onLastWindowClosed = ::exitApplication)

    for (document in documents) {
        key(document.id) {
            Tab(workspace, id = document.id, title = document.name) { Editor(document) }
            DropClosedTab(workspace, documents, document.id)
        }
    }
}
```

`TabWindows` opens one window per group of tabs, with the strip in its title bar and the selected
tab as its body. Never declare a `Tab` inside a window.

When the user closes a tab, the workspace forgets it but your list still declares it. Drop it
from the list, or the next composition registers it again:

```kotlin
@Composable
private fun DropClosedTab(workspace: TabWorkspace, documents: MutableList<Document>, id: String) {
    val closed = workspace.tab(id) == null
    LaunchedEffect(closed) { if (closed) documents.removeAll { it.id == id } }
}
```

## Tab and TabWindows parameters

`Tab(workspace, id, title, group = null) { … }` opens in `group` on first declaration, else in the
window focused last, else in a new window. The selected tab's `title` is the window title. The
body runs with `TabScope`: `workspace`, `tab`, `select()`, `close()`.

| `TabWindows` parameter | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `workspace` | required | The `TabWorkspace` |
| `strip` | `{ TabStrip() }` | One window's strip, with `TabStripScope` as receiver |
| `dragGhost` | `{ TabDragGhostCard(it) }` | The card under the pointer while a tab leaves its strip |
| `nativeContextMenu` | `true` | Native context menu for text fields |
| `windowWrapper` | `{ it() }` | Wraps each window, strip included: `WindowBackground`, a themed `Surface` |
| `windowBodyWrapper` | `{ it() }` | Wraps what is under the strip: a `DockLayout`, a status bar |
| `onLastWindowClosed` | `{}` | Called each time the workspace goes from holding tabs to holding none |

Both wrappers receive the window's `NucleusDecoratedWindowScope` and must invoke their lambda.
Set the theme around `TabWindows`, not inside a window: the workspace passes those locals to
every window it opens.

```kotlin
MaterialTheme(colorScheme = colors) {
    CompositionLocalProvider(LocalTitleBarStyle provides rememberMaterialTitleBarStyle(colors)) {
        TabWindows(workspace, onLastWindowClosed = ::exitApplication)
        // Tab declarations
    }
}
```

`rememberTabWorkspace(defaultWindowSize, captureThumbnails)` takes the size of new windows
(960 × 640 dp by default) and whether to capture thumbnails (`false`).

## Drag tabs

With the stock strip, the user drags a tab along the strip to reorder it, out of the window to
open a new one, or onto another window's strip to merge it. Dragging the only tab of a window
moves the window itself. A tab pulled out of a maximized window opens at `defaultWindowSize`.

`Modifier.tabDragHandle(workspace, tab)` is the grip `TabStrip` puts on every tab. On native
Wayland it reorders inside the strip, then hands off to a platform drag when the pointer leaves:
`draggedTab` is set while `dragKind` is still `null` during the local phase. A custom strip in the
title bar also applies `Modifier.noWindowDrag()` to each grip, so the compositor's window move
does not swallow the gesture.

For a right-to-left strip, provide `LayoutDirection.Rtl` around `TabStrip`. Reorder and drop
indices follow it.

## Customize the stock strip

| `TabStrip` parameter | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `reorderAnimation` | spring, `StiffnessMediumLow` | How a tab travels along the strip; `null` moves it at once |
| `hoverPreview` | `null` | The card under a hovered tab. `TabHoverPreview.Default` for the stock card |
| `tabLeading` / `tabTrailing` | `null` | Per-tab slots around the title: a file icon, a modified dot |
| `dropGhostCard` | `{ TabDropGhostCard(it) }` | The card in the slot a tab from another window would fill |
| `trailing` | `{}` | After the last tab: a new-tab button (a tab dropped on it is appended) |

```kotlin
TabWindows(
    workspace = workspace,
    strip = {
        TabStrip(
            hoverPreview = TabHoverPreview.Default,
            tabTrailing = { tab -> if (tab.id in modified) Text("●") },
            trailing = { IconButton(onClick = ::openDocument) { Text("+") } },
        )
    },
)
```

`TabStripScope` exposes `workspace`, `group`, `tabs` (in strip order), `dropGhost` and
`hoveredTab`.

## Write a strip from scratch

A strip from another design system needs three modifiers:

| Modifier | Apply to |
| --- | --- |
| `Modifier.tabStripGeometry(workspace, group)` | The element spanning the whole strip |
| `Modifier.tabSlot(group, index)` | Each tab, in strip order |
| `Modifier.tabDragHandle(workspace, tab)` | Each tab's grip |

While a tab from another window hovers the strip, `dropGhost` holds a
`TabDropGhost(index, width, tab)`: compose `TabDropGhostCard(ghost)` at `index`. Add
`TabHoverPreviewPopup(preview)` once for hover cards. `jewel-tabs-demo` wraps Jewel's `TabStrip`
this way.

## Draw previews

**Thumbnails.** `TabEntry.thumbnail` is an `ImageBitmap?`. With `captureThumbnails = true` the
workspace records each window's selected tab; call `captureThumbnail(tabId)` after a visible
change. You can also assign one yourself before the tab is shown. `NativeView` and `TextureView`
content is missing from captures. `TabPreview(tab, modifier, contentScale, placeholder)` draws
the thumbnail.

**Hover cards.** `TabHoverPreview(delay, offset, nativeLayer, content)` describes the card.
`delay` defaults to 650 ms; `nativeLayer = false` draws the card inside the window, clipped. The stock card is
`TabHoverPreviewCard(modifier, subtitle = null)`:

```kotlin
val preview = remember {
    TabHoverPreview { TabHoverPreviewCard(subtitle = { Text(pathOf(tab.id), maxLines = 1) }) }
}
TabStrip(hoverPreview = preview)
```

**Drag and drop cards.** Draw `TabWindows(dragGhost)` and `TabStrip(dropGhostCard)` with the same
composable, built on `TabGhostCard(tab, modifier)`, so the tab lands as it travelled.
`dragGhost` runs outside `windowWrapper` and never on native Wayland.

## Drive tabs from code

| Call | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `select(tabId)` | Make it the visible tab of its group |
| `close(tabId)` | Remove it, state included; an empty group closes its window |
| `move(tabId, group, index = null)` | Move it into `group` at `index` (`null` appends) and select it |
| `reorder(tabId, index)` | Move it within its group |
| `tearOff(tabId, screenRectPx, scaleFactor)` | Open it in a new window at a screen rect in physical pixels |

Read `tabs`, `tab(id)`, `groups`, `group(id)`, `activeGroup` (where new tabs open),
`groupOf(window)`, `tabsOf(group)`, `selectedTab(group)`, and the drag in flight with
`draggedTab`, `dropPreview`, `dragGhost`, `dragKind`. A closed tab is gone: declaring it again
creates a new tab in the active window.

## Save and restore the layout

`snapshot()` returns a `TabLayoutSnapshot(groups)`. Each `TabGroupSnapshot` holds `id`, `tabIds`,
`selectedId`, `position` and `size`. `restore(snapshot)` moves the tabs and places the windows,
including tabs declared later. It applies once; call it again after a tab is closed and
redeclared.

## Compose tabs with satellites

Give each tab window its own `SatelliteWorkspace`, keyed by group id, and let its satellites draw
the selected tab. A tab change then only swaps content.

```kotlin
TabWindows(
    workspace = tabs,
    windowWrapper = { content ->
        tabs.groupOf(nucleusWindow.unsafe.taoWindow)?.let { JoinSatelliteWorkspace(panesOf(it.id)) }
        content()
    },
    windowBodyWrapper = { body ->
        val group = tabs.groupOf(nucleusWindow.unsafe.taoWindow)
        if (group == null) body() else DockLayout(panesOf(group.id), Modifier.fillMaxSize()) { body() }
    },
)

for (group in rememberTabGroups(tabs)) {
    key(group.id) {
        val document = tabs.selectedTab(group)?.let { documentOf(it.id) }
        Satellite(panesOf(group.id), id = "inspector-${group.id}", title = "Inspector") {
            Inspector(document)
        }
    }
}
```

`rememberTabGroups` mirrors `workspace.groups` through an effect, since `Tab` creates groups
during the composition that reads the list:

```kotlin
@Composable
fun rememberTabGroups(workspace: TabWorkspace): List<TabWindowGroup> {
    var groups by remember(workspace) { mutableStateOf(workspace.groups.toList()) }
    LaunchedEffect(workspace) { snapshotFlow { workspace.groups.toList() }.collect { groups = it } }
    return groups
}
```

Open and close those satellites from a `LaunchedEffect`, never during composition.
`tab-satellites-demo` and `reader-dock-demo` show both setups.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- Only the selected tab of a window is composed, so `captureThumbnail` reaches only tabs on screen.
- Another window's strip counts as entered once the ghost card reaches it; the strip under the
  pointer still wins.
- On native Wayland, a tab leaving its strip moves to a platform drag-and-drop session, and each
  other strip resolves the drop in its own coordinates.
- A tab change rebuilds neither wrapper. A tab is clipped to its slot only while it opens or
  closes, so a carried card is never cut.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## What's next

- [Satellites](/docs/multi-window/satellites): palettes, headers and owners.
- [Docking](/docs/multi-window/docking): the `DockLayout` a tab window can host.
- [Toolkits](/docs/toolkits): title-bar styles the stock strip picks up.

# Trackpad gestures

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/input/trackpad-gestures

Handle trackpad scrolling, pinch-to-zoom and rotation with standard Compose modifiers.

Trackpad gestures reach Compose as standard pointer events. `Modifier.scrollable`, the lazy lists
and `Modifier.transformable` handle them with no extra code, and you add no dependency beyond
`nucleus-application`.

## Events per gesture

| Gesture | macOS | Windows | Linux |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Two-finger scroll | `PanStart` / `PanMove` / `PanEnd` | `Scroll` | `Scroll` |
| Mouse wheel | `Scroll` | `Scroll` | `Scroll` |
| Pinch, Ctrl + wheel | `ScaleStart` / `ScaleChange` / `ScaleEnd` | `Scale*` | `Scale*` |
| Rotation | two `Touch` pointers | none | two `Touch` pointers |

## Scroll

Scrolling containers work as they are. Only a custom `pointerInput` handler needs care: on macOS a
trackpad swipe arrives as `PanMove`, so a handler that listens for `Scroll` alone misses it.

```kotlin
Modifier.pointerInput(Unit) {
    awaitPointerEventScope {
        while (true) {
            val event = awaitPointerEvent()
            val change = event.changes.first()
            when (event.type) {
                PointerEventType.PanMove -> move(change.panOffset)
                PointerEventType.Scroll -> move(change.scrollDelta)
                else -> Unit
            }
        }
    }
}
```

To receive every trackpad step as `Scroll` instead, start the JVM with
`-Dnucleus.tao.trackpadPanEvents=false`.

## Zoom with a pinch

`detectTransformGestures` no longer sees a pinch. Use `Modifier.transformable` or listen for the
`Scale*` events. See [Migrate from 2.x](/docs/migrate/from-2.x#handle-pinch-and-pan-events).

```kotlin
@Composable
fun ZoomableImage() {
    var scale by remember { mutableFloatStateOf(1f) }
    val state = rememberTransformableState { zoomChange, _, _ -> scale *= zoomChange }
    Box(
        Modifier
            .fillMaxSize()
            .graphicsLayer(scaleX = scale, scaleY = scale)
            .transformable(state),
    )
}
```

In a custom handler, read `PointerInputChange.scaleFactor` on `ScaleChange`. It is a ratio per
event: above `1f` zooms in, below `1f` zooms out.

## Rotate

`Modifier.transformable` and `detectTransformGestures` read the rotation angle on macOS and Linux.
Windows reports no trackpad rotation. A pinch and a rotation never run at the same time: the
gesture that starts first keeps the trackpad until it ends.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- `panOffset` uses the same 10 dp per unit that Compose Desktop applies to a wheel notch, so a pan
  and a notch scroll the same distance.
- `PanEnd` arrives after macOS's momentum tail, so Compose does not start a second fling.
- Ctrl + wheel has no end phase: `ScaleEnd` follows 120 ms after the last tick.
- On Linux, GDK reports scale and rotation as one gesture. It starts as a pinch, and rotation takes
  over once it has turned 10° with the zoom within ±10%.
- `TaoWindow.onTrackpadGesture` exposes the raw stream (macOS and Windows). Registering a listener
  replaces the one `DecoratedWindow` uses, which stops pinch and rotation events for that window.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## API reference

| Symbol | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `PointerEventType.PanStart` / `PanMove` / `PanEnd` | macOS trackpad scroll |
| `PointerInputChange.panOffset` | Pan delta in pixels |
| `PointerEventType.ScaleStart` / `ScaleChange` / `ScaleEnd` | Pinch and Ctrl + wheel |
| `PointerInputChange.scaleFactor` | Zoom ratio per event |
| `-Dnucleus.tao.trackpadPanEvents=false` | Send trackpad pans as `Scroll` |

## What's next

- [Pen and touch input](/docs/input/pen-stylus): touchscreen contacts and pressure.
- [Pointer icons](/docs/input/pointer-icons): cursors beyond the four Compose defines.
- [Migrate from 2.x](/docs/migrate/from-2.x): every behavior change in 3.0.

# Pen and touch input

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/input/pen-stylus

Read touchscreen and pen contacts, with pressure, from Compose pointer events.

Touchscreen and pen contacts reach Compose as pointers of type `PointerType.Touch`. You read them
with the same `pointerInput` modifier as mouse input, and you add nothing beyond
`nucleus-application`.

## Draw with pressure

```kotlin
Modifier.pointerInput(Unit) {
    awaitPointerEventScope {
        while (true) {
            val change = awaitPointerEvent().changes.first()
            if (change.type == PointerType.Touch) {
                addPoint(change.position, change.pressure)
                change.consume()
            }
        }
    }
}
```

Gesture detectors, `consume()` and hit testing treat these contacts like any other Compose
pointer.

## Platform support

| Platform | Arrives as | Pressure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Windows | `PointerType.Touch` | Reported when the digitizer supports it |
| Linux (Wayland and X11) | `PointerType.Touch` | Always `1f` |
| macOS | Mouse | Not reported |

- Treat `pressure == 1f` as "average or unknown". Most consumer touchscreens report `1f`.
- Nucleus never produces `PointerType.Stylus` or `PointerType.Eraser`, and `PointerInputChange`
  carries no tilt or barrel rotation. A pen and a finger differ only by pressure, on Windows.
- A finger dragged on the title bar moves the window on Windows and Linux. On Linux, a finger on a
  window edge resizes it.

## What's next

- [Trackpad gestures](/docs/input/trackpad-gestures): pans, pinch-to-zoom and rotation.
- [Linux and Wayland](/docs/windows/linux-wayland): compositor behavior on Linux.
- [Accessibility](/docs/input/accessibility): expose your UI to screen readers.

# Drag and drop

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/input/drag-and-drop

Receive files dropped on a window and drag files or text out of it with the Compose drag-and-drop API.

Drag and drop uses the standard Compose modifiers, `Modifier.dragAndDropTarget` and
`Modifier.dragAndDropSource`, and comes with `nucleus-application`. Both need
`@OptIn(ExperimentalComposeUiApi::class)`.

## Receive dropped files

```kotlin
val target = remember {
    object : DragAndDropTarget {
        override fun onDrop(event: DragAndDropEvent): Boolean {
            @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
            val files = event.awtTransferable
                .getTransferData(DataFlavor.javaFileListFlavor) as List<File>
            onFiles(files)
            return files.isNotEmpty()
        }
    }
}

Box(Modifier.fillMaxSize().dragAndDropTarget(shouldStartDragAndDrop = { true }, target = target))
```

Return `true` from `onDrop` to accept the data. `DataFlavor.stringFlavor` returns the same paths
joined by newlines.

- Inbound drops carry files only. Text, HTML and URL drops are not delivered.
- The file list is available in `onDrop`. The enter, move and exit callbacks receive an empty list.
- [`TrayApp`](/docs/os/tray/tray-app) popups accept drops through the same modifier.

## Drag data out of the window

Wrap an AWT `Transferable` that offers `javaFileListFlavor`, `stringFlavor`, or both:

```kotlin
Modifier.dragAndDropSource { _ ->
    DragAndDropTransferData(
        transferable = DragAndDropTransferable(StringSelection("Hello from Nucleus")),
        supportedActions = listOf(DragAndDropTransferAction.Copy),
        onTransferCompleted = { action -> /* null when cancelled */ },
    )
}
```

A transferable with neither files nor text does not start a drag. Your window keeps drawing while
the cursor is outside it.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- Nucleus installs no AWT `DropTarget`, and reading `awtTransferable` does not start the AWT
  toolkit.
- To debug a drag that does not start, read `TaoDnDDiagnostics.lastMessage`
  (`dev.nucleusframework.window.tao`): it holds the last reason a drag was skipped.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## What's next

- [Pointer icons](/docs/input/pointer-icons): show a grab or not-allowed cursor during a drag.
- [Tabs](/docs/multi-window/tabs): tear-off and merge built on the same drag session.
- [Trackpad gestures](/docs/input/trackpad-gestures): pans and pinch-to-zoom.

# Pointer icons

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/input/pointer-icons

Show grab, move, wait, help and resize cursors with TaoPointerIcons and Modifier.pointerHoverIcon.

`TaoPointerIcons` (`dev.nucleusframework.window.tao`, part of `nucleus-application`) adds the
cursors Compose does not define in common code. Pass them to `Modifier.pointerHoverIcon`:

```kotlin
Modifier.pointerHoverIcon(if (dragging) TaoPointerIcons.Grabbing else TaoPointerIcons.Grab)
```

Compose's own `PointerIcon.Default`, `Text`, `Hand` and `Crosshair` keep working.

## Available icons

| Icon | Typical use |
| --- | --- |
| `Grab` / `Grabbing` | Drag handle on hover / while dragging |
| `Move` | An element that will move |
| `NotAllowed` | A refused drop |
| `Wait` | The app ignores input |
| `Progress` | Busy, still interactive |
| `Help` | Contextual help |
| `ResizeEastWest` / `ResizeNorthSouth` | Splitters and window edges |

Each icon uses the platform's own shape, or the arrow where the platform has none.

## Replace AWT cursors

`PointerIcon(Cursor(...))` maps only the predefined AWT text, hand, crosshair, wait, move and
resize types. Other AWT cursors, including `Toolkit.createCustomCursor` images, show the arrow.

| 2.x with AWT | 3.0 |
| --- | --- |
| `PointerIcon(Cursor(Cursor.MOVE_CURSOR))` | `TaoPointerIcons.Move` |
| `PointerIcon(Cursor(Cursor.WAIT_CURSOR))` | `TaoPointerIcons.Wait` |
| `PointerIcon(Cursor(Cursor.E_RESIZE_CURSOR))` | `TaoPointerIcons.ResizeEastWest` |
| `PointerIcon(Cursor(Cursor.N_RESIZE_CURSOR))` | `TaoPointerIcons.ResizeNorthSouth` |

## What's next

- [Drag and drop](/docs/input/drag-and-drop): pair `Grab` and `NotAllowed` with a drop target.
- [Docking](/docs/multi-window/docking): splitters that use the resize cursors.
- [Migrate from 2.x](/docs/migrate/from-2.x): every behavior change in 3.0.

# Accessibility

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/input/accessibility

Expose your Compose semantics to VoiceOver, Narrator, Orca and UI automation tools.

Nucleus exposes your Compose semantics to VoiceOver on macOS, Narrator on Windows and Orca on
Linux. You write standard Compose semantics and screen readers read them. Every `DecoratedWindow`
comes with the bridge, part of `nucleus-application`.

## Make your UI accessible

Attach Compose semantics to your composables. You never build accessibility nodes by hand:

```kotlin
Button(onClick = { count++ }, modifier = Modifier.testTag("increment")) {
    Text("Increment")
}

Image(
    painter = painterResource("logo.png"),
    contentDescription = "Company logo",
)

Text(
    "Loading",
    modifier = Modifier.semantics { contentDescription = "Loading, please wait" },
)
```

A screen reader sees the `Button` as a button it can activate and the `Image` as an image labeled
"Company logo". Nodes marked `InvisibleToUser` or `HideFromAccessibility` stay out of the OS tree.

When a screen reader activates, increments or edits an element, Nucleus runs the matching Compose
`SemanticsActions` handler on the UI thread. A read-only text field does not offer text editing to the screen reader.

## Find elements from UI automation

`Modifier.testTag(...)` becomes a stable identifier that UI automation tools can query instead of
the visible label:

| Platform | Attribute |
| --- | --- |
| macOS | `AXIdentifier` |
| Windows | `UIA_AutomationIdPropertyId` |
| Linux | AccessKit author id |

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- Nucleus maps the semantics tree to NSAccessibility on macOS, and through AccessKit to UI
  Automation on Windows and AT-SPI on Linux.
- Nucleus walks the tree only while an assistive technology is attached. Until then, scrolling and
  animation pay nothing for the bridge.
- On Windows and Linux, updates carry only the changed nodes. macOS rebuilds the full tree on each
  update.
- A window move does not trigger a new push: node frames use window-local coordinates.
- `TaoA11yRole`, `TaoA11yFlag` and `TaoA11yAction` in `dev.nucleusframework.window.tao` list the
  roles, states and actions a screen reader can see. Your app does not construct or read them.
  `MULTI_SELECTABLE`, `EXPANDED_TRUE` and `EXPANDED_FALSE` reach Linux only.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## What's next

- [Windows](/docs/windows): the `DecoratedWindow` that installs the bridge.
- [Linux and Wayland](/docs/windows/linux-wayland): Linux windowing, where AT-SPI goes through AccessKit.
- [Pen and touch input](/docs/input/pen-stylus): touchscreen and pen contacts.

---

# Native views

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/native-content/native-views

Embed an NSView, HWND or GtkWidget inside a Compose layout with NativeView.

`NativeView` embeds a platform-native view in a Compose layout, the desktop counterpart of
`AndroidView` and `UIKitView`. You hand it an `NSView*`, `HWND` or `GtkWidget*`, and Nucleus keeps
it on its layout slot until the composable leaves. It comes with `nucleus-application`.

## Embed a native view

Return a `NucleusPlatformView` from `factory`:

```kotlin
@Composable
fun BrowserPane(url: String) {
    NativeView(
        factory = {
            // createNativeWebView is your own interop code returning an NSView* as a Long.
            val handle = createNativeWebView(url)
            nucleusNsPlatformView(
                handle = { handle },
                onDispose = { releaseNativeWebView(handle) },
            )
        },
        modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize(),
    )
}
```

You create the native view; `factory` runs once. The view follows its slot through layout
changes, scrolling and resizes. Use `nucleusHwndPlatformView` on Windows and
`nucleusGtkPlatformView` on Linux. On another OS, `NativeView` renders an empty `Box(modifier)`,
so one call site per platform is enough. You can also implement `NucleusPlatformView.NsView`,
`HWnd` or `GtkWidget` on your own class.

On Linux, `NativeView` requires Wayland. Under X11 the widget stays hidden behind the window
surface and its rectangle shows the desktop.

## Release the view

`dispose()`, or the factory's `onDispose`, runs after the host has detached the handle. Free the
native view there. On Linux, hold your own reference to the widget (`g_object_ref_sink`) while
you use the handle and drop it in `dispose()`, or GTK finalizes it on detach.

## Overlay Compose content

The `content` slot draws Compose UI on top of the native view:

```kotlin
NativeView(
    factory = { /* ... */ },
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize(),
) {
    // The button handles its own clicks; clicks elsewhere reach the native view.
    Button(onClick = { /* reload */ }) { Text("Reload") }
}
```

Compose hit-tests first: anything drawn over the view keeps its pointer events. Events Compose
does not consume go to the native view, trackpad pans included. `Popup`s draw above the view.

## Clip to rounded corners

`Modifier.clip()` does not reach native views. Pass `cornerRadius = 12.dp` instead; `Dp.Infinity`
gives a circle. `cornerRadius` has no effect on Linux: draw a rounded border in `content`.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- Compose clears the view's rectangle to transparent, and the native content shows through.
- macOS: the `NSView` sits below the Compose Metal layer. Moves apply in the same frame as the
  Compose geometry.
- Windows: the child `HWND` sits under the window, and a DirectComposition overlay renders Compose
  above it.
- Linux: the widget sits in the window's GTK content, and the compositor blends it through the GL
  surface. X11 does not blend a child window's alpha, hence the Wayland requirement. GTK 3 has no
  per-widget rounded clip.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## API reference

| `NativeView` parameter | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `factory` | required | `() -> NucleusPlatformView`, called once |
| `modifier` | `Modifier` | Sizes and places the slot |
| `update` | `{}` | Runs after every recomposition. Push new state into the view here |
| `cornerRadius` | `Dp.Unspecified` | Rounded clip; unspecified applies none |
| `content` | `{}` | Compose overlay drawn over the view |

The factories take a `handle: () -> Long` lambda, read each time the host needs the pointer, and
optional callbacks:

| Member | Factory callback | Called when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `resize(widthPx, heightPx)` | `onResize` | The view's size changes. |
| `setBounds(xPx, yPx, widthPx, heightPx)` | `onSetBounds` | The frame changes. For views that draw outside a window rect, such as WebView2. |
| `setCornerRadius(radiusPx)` | `onSetCornerRadius` | The rounded clip changes. |
| `clearFocus()` | `onClearFocus` | The window or a Compose layer takes focus. |
| `dispose()` | `onDispose` | After detach. Release your native resources. |

On Windows, a `hwndHandle` of `0L` is valid for a view with no child window, such as WebView2 in
composition mode; it drives its visual through `setBounds` and `setCornerRadius`.

`Modifier.consumeOverlayPointerEvents()` is deprecated and does nothing: use
`Modifier.pointerHoverIcon` for its `cursor` argument.

## What's next

- [WebView](/docs/webview): a ready-made WebView built on `NativeView`.
- [TextureView](/docs/native-content/texture-view): show GPU frames from an external producer.
- [Pointer icons](/docs/input/pointer-icons): cursors for the Compose overlay.

# TextureView

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/native-content/texture-view

Draw a GPU texture from an external producer inside the Compose scene, with no CPU frame copy.

`TextureView` draws a GPU texture that another component produces, such as a video decoder, a
camera pipeline or a game engine, inside the Compose scene. No frame goes through the CPU, and
z-order, clipping, `graphicsLayer` and scrolling apply as for any composable. It comes with
`nucleus-application` and handles no input: use [`NativeView`](/docs/native-content/native-views)
for interactive widgets, or [`TaoGpuRenderContext`](/docs/native-content/gpu-render-context) to
render on the scene's own device.

## Show a texture

Wrap your producer's platform handle in a `TextureViewSource`, place a `TextureView`, and call
`controller.markFrameAvailable()` after each finished frame:

```kotlin
@Composable
fun VideoPane(source: TextureViewSource?) {
    val controller = rememberTextureViewController()
    DisposableEffect(source) {
        // Start the producer; it calls controller.markFrameAvailable() after each frame.
        onDispose { /* stop the producer */ }
    }
    TextureView(
        source = source,
        controller = controller,
        modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize(),
        contentScale = ContentScale.Fit,
    )
}
```

`markFrameAvailable()` is safe from any thread and re-runs only the draw pass. It does not pace
your producer: throttle it to the display yourself. `contentScale`, `alignment` and
`filterQuality` behave as on `Image`. When `source` is `null`, belongs to another platform, or
fails to import, `TextureView` renders an empty `Box(modifier)`.

## Platform sources

**Windows**

```kotlin
val source = nucleusD3D11SharedTextureSource(
    sharedHandle = dxgiSharedHandle, // IDXGIResource::GetSharedHandle
    widthPx = width,
    heightPx = height,
)
```

- Pass a legacy handle from `GetSharedHandle`. NT handles (`D3D11_RESOURCE_MISC_SHARED_NTHANDLE`)
  do not import.
- Use `R8G8B8A8_UNORM` or a compatible RGBA8 format with premultiplied alpha, at `widthPx` ×
  `heightPx`.
- With `D3D11_RESOURCE_MISC_SHARED_KEYEDMUTEX` (recommended), bracket producer writes with
  `AcquireSync(0)` / `ReleaseSync(0)`; frames never tear. With plain `D3D11_RESOURCE_MISC_SHARED`
  there is no copy, but call `Flush()` after each frame.

See [mediafoundation-demo](https://github.com/NucleusFramework/Nucleus/tree/main/examples/mediafoundation-demo).

**macOS**

```kotlin
// Shareable buffer, from any device or process
val surfaceSource = nucleusIOSurfaceTextureSource(ioSurface = ioSurfaceRef, widthPx = width, heightPx = height)

// Metal texture from the same process
val metalSource = nucleusMetalTextureSource(metalTexture = mtlTexture, widthPx = width, heightPx = height)
```

- Use 32-bit `BGRA` or `RGBA` (sRGB included) with premultiplied alpha, at `widthPx` × `heightPx`.
- Finish producer writes (`commit` and `waitUntilCompleted`, or double buffering) before
  `markFrameAvailable()`.
- The source retains the `IOSurface`, so your producer can release its own hold.
- A Metal texture must be render-target capable on the window's device or backed by an
  `IOSurface`; otherwise pass an `IOSurface` source.
- On a Mac with only a discrete Intel GPU, the import fails and you get an empty box.

See [avfoundation-demo](https://github.com/NucleusFramework/Nucleus/tree/main/examples/avfoundation-demo).

**Linux**

```kotlin
// Packed 32-bit RGB DMA-BUF
val rgb = nucleusDmaBufTextureSource(
    fd = dmaBufFd, widthPx = width, heightPx = height, stride = stride,
    fourcc = NucleusDrmFormat.ARGB8888,
)

// Three-plane YUV from a hardware decoder
val yuv = nucleusYuvDmaBufTextureSource(
    widthPx = width,
    heightPx = height,
    format = NucleusYuvFormat.I420,
    planes = listOf(
        NucleusDmaBufPlane(fd = yFd, stride = yStride),
        NucleusDmaBufPlane(fd = uFd, stride = uStride),
        NucleusDmaBufPlane(fd = vFd, stride = vStride),
    ),
    colorSpace = NucleusYuvColorSpace.BT709_LIMITED,
)
```

- RGB FourCC: `ARGB8888`, `XRGB8888`, `ABGR8888` or `XBGR8888`. You keep ownership of `fd`.
- YUV supports `I420` and `YV12`. NV12 and NV21 are not supported.
- `NucleusYuvColorSpace`: `BT601_LIMITED`, `BT601_FULL`, `BT709_LIMITED`, `BT709_FULL`. A wrong
  value shows as washed-out or oversaturated color.
- `controller.markFrameAvailable(acquireFenceFd)` hands over a `sync_file` fence instead of
  finishing on the CPU. It requires `EGL_ANDROID_native_fence_sync`.

See [gstreamer-demo](https://github.com/NucleusFramework/Nucleus/tree/main/examples/gstreamer-demo).

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- Nucleus imports the producer's allocation on the window's GPU and samples it in the draw pass.
  `TextureView`s that share one `TextureViewSource` share one import.
- The Windows keyed-mutex path copies each frame once on the GPU; macOS always copies once.
- NV12 and NV21 fail because the Skia build Compose ships cannot sample an interleaved chroma
  plane. EGL takes its own reference to a DMA-BUF `fd` at import.
- `rememberTextureViewController()` releases a pending fence when the composition leaves. Other
  platforms ignore a fence fd and leave it yours.
- `D3D11TestTextureProducer`, `MetalTestTextureProducer` and `DmaBufTestTextureProducer` produce
  test frames for demos and CI.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## API reference

`TextureView(source, modifier, controller = null, filterQuality = FilterQuality.Low,
contentScale = ContentScale.FillBounds, alignment = Alignment.Center)`

| Factory | Platform | Handle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `nucleusD3D11SharedTextureSource(sharedHandle, widthPx, heightPx)` | Windows | Legacy DXGI shared handle |
| `nucleusIOSurfaceTextureSource(ioSurface, widthPx, heightPx)` | macOS | `IOSurfaceRef` |
| `nucleusMetalTextureSource(metalTexture, widthPx, heightPx)` | macOS | `id<MTLTexture>` |
| `nucleusDmaBufTextureSource(fd, widthPx, heightPx, stride, fourcc, offset, modifier)` | Linux | Single-plane DMA-BUF |
| `nucleusEglImageTextureSource(eglImage, widthPx, heightPx)` | Linux | `EGLImageKHR` |
| `nucleusYuvDmaBufTextureSource(widthPx, heightPx, format, planes, colorSpace)` | Linux | Planar YUV DMA-BUF |

Handles are raw pointers passed as `Long`. An import failure only shows as an empty box: check
formats and dimensions first. `TextureViewController.NO_FENCE` is `-1`.

## What's next

- [GPU render context](/docs/native-content/gpu-render-context): render on the scene's own device.
- [Native views](/docs/native-content/native-views): embed interactive `NSView`, `HWND` or `GtkWidget` content.
- [Windows](/docs/windows): open the window that hosts the texture.

# GPU render context

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/native-content/gpu-render-context

Give an in-process renderer the scene's Skia DirectContext and GPU device, so it draws without a second device or a per-frame copy.

`TaoGpuRenderContext` publishes the GPU context of the enclosing Compose surface: the Skia
`DirectContext` the scene draws with and the native device behind it. An in-process renderer,
such as a map engine, a 3D viewport or a charting library, allocates its render targets there,
and Compose samples them with no shared handle or copy. It comes with `nucleus-application`.

For a producer on its own device or in another process, use
[`TextureView`](/docs/native-content/texture-view).

## Get the context

Call `rememberTaoGpuRenderContext()` inside a surface that owns a GPU context: `DecoratedWindow`
content, a native popup layer, a `NativeView` overlay or a tray panel. It returns `null` during
bring-up and teardown, and when no hardware context exists.

```kotlin
@Composable
fun MapViewport() {
    val renderContext = rememberTaoGpuRenderContext() ?: return
    // A rebuilt context is a new instance: key renderer state on it.
    val renderer = remember(renderContext) { MapEngineRenderer(renderContext) }
    DisposableEffect(renderContext) {
        onDispose { renderContext.runOnGpuThread { renderer.releaseGpuResources() } }
    }
    LaunchedEffect(renderer) {
        while (true) {
            withFrameNanos { renderer.renderFrame() }   // GPU work inside the callback
        }
    }
}
```

## Pick the backend

| Type | Platforms | `backend` | Extra member |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `TaoMetalRenderContext` | macOS | `TaoRenderBackend.METAL` | `metalDevicePtr`: the `id<MTLDevice>` |
| `TaoOpenGlRenderContext` | Linux, Windows | `TaoRenderBackend.OPENGL` | `withContextCurrent { }`: binds the surface's GL context |

Both expose `skiaContext` and `runOnGpuThread { }`. On Windows, `OPENGL` means ANGLE's GLES 3 on
Direct3D 11: resolve entry points through ANGLE's `eglGetProcAddress`.

## Respect ownership and lifetime

- Every handle is borrowed: never retain, release or free it.
- The context is rebuilt on window detach, a Wayland hide and show, or popup and tray panel
  teardown, and `rememberTaoGpuRenderContext()` then returns a new instance or `null`. Key state
  with `remember(renderContext)` and free GPU resources in a `DisposableEffect(renderContext)`,
  inside `runOnGpuThread` or `withContextCurrent`.
- Call every member from the UI thread (the main thread on macOS).

## Pace frames

Issue GPU work inside the `withFrameNanos` callback, or during composition, layout or draw. On
Linux, code that runs after the `withFrameNanos` suspension gets `null` from `withContextCurrent`
almost every vsync. `withContextCurrent` is safe to nest.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- On macOS, `runOnGpuThread` hops to the render thread that owns the Metal context and blocks
  until the action returns. On Linux and Windows it runs inline on the event-loop thread.
- On Linux the host hands the EGL context to a swap thread for `eglSwapBuffers` right after each
  frame, hence the pacing rule.
- `withContextCurrent` restores the previous context and resets Skia's GL state cache, so your GL
  calls do not corrupt the scene's frame.
- While a scene has live `TextureView` imports or GPU context consumers, Nucleus keeps VSync on
  through the Windows modal move and resize loop and Linux resize bursts.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## What's next

- [TextureView](/docs/native-content/texture-view): import GPU frames from an external producer.
- [Native views](/docs/native-content/native-views): embed interactive native widgets.
- [Threading](/docs/concepts/threading): the UI thread these calls run on.

# Toolkits

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/toolkits

macOS 26, Fluent, Yaru, Jewel, and Material restyle the Nucleus window for each desktop design language.

A toolkit styles the window chrome and, for the full design systems, the widgets inside it.
macOS 26, Fluent and Yaru are full design systems in their own repositories. Jewel and Material
style the chrome only, and ship with Nucleus.

## Compare the toolkits

| Toolkit | Native to | Artifacts | Ships with |
|---------|-----------|-----------|------------|
| [macOS 26](/docs/toolkits/macos) | macOS Tahoe | `dev.nucleusframework:compose-macos-ui` | Its own repo |
| [Fluent](/docs/toolkits/fluent) | Windows 11 | `dev.nucleusframework.composefluent:fluent` + `decorated-window-fluent` | Its own repo |
| [Yaru](/docs/toolkits/yaru) | Ubuntu / GNOME | `dev.nucleusframework.yarucompose:yaru` + `yaru-decorated-window` | Its own repo |
| [Jewel](/docs/toolkits/jewel) | IntelliJ Platform | `dev.nucleusframework:nucleus.decorated-window-jewel` | Nucleus |
| [Material 2](/docs/toolkits/material) | Any | `dev.nucleusframework:nucleus.decorated-window-material2` | Nucleus |
| [Material 3](/docs/toolkits/material) | Any | `dev.nucleusframework:nucleus.decorated-window-material3` | Nucleus |

The three design-system repos version independently of Nucleus. Pick a release whose README names
your Nucleus line. Live galleries:
[macOS 26](https://nucleusframework.github.io/compose-macos-26-ui/),
[Fluent](https://nucleusframework.github.io/compose-fluent-ui/),
[Yaru](https://nucleusframework.github.io/yaru-compose-ui/).

## Open a toolkit window

Call the toolkit window inside `nucleusApplication { }`. Where the theme goes depends on the
toolkit:

```kotlin
fun main() = nucleusApplication {
    // Fluent, Jewel, Material: the theme wraps the window
    FluentTheme {
        FluentDecoratedWindow(onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication, title = "Settings") {
            FluentTitleBar { /* … */ }
            App()
        }
    }
    // macOS 26, Yaru: the theme goes inside the window
    MacosDecoratedWindow(onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication, title = "Mail") {
        MacosTheme { App() }
    }
}
```

Each toolkit page lists its dependencies and imports.

The Jewel and Material windows and dialogs exist only as `NucleusApplicationScope` extensions. The
overloads on Compose's `ApplicationScope`, and the top-level Material 2 and Jewel dialogs, are gone.
See [Migrate from Nucleus 2.x](/docs/migrate/from-2.x).

To build custom chrome without a toolkit, use [`WindowScaffold`](/docs/windows/window-scaffold).

## What's next

- [macOS 26](/docs/toolkits/macos): Liquid Glass materials and the macOS 26 widget set.
- [Jewel](/docs/toolkits/jewel): IntelliJ Platform chrome.
- [Material 2 and 3](/docs/toolkits/material): chrome from a Compose `MaterialTheme`.
- [Windows](/docs/windows): the `DecoratedWindow` API every toolkit wraps.

# macOS 26

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/toolkits/macos

A Compose Multiplatform macOS 26 design system with Liquid Glass materials and a Nucleus decorated window.

[compose-macos-26-ui](https://github.com/NucleusFramework/compose-macos-26-ui) is a Compose
Multiplatform design system for the macOS 26 look, with a desktop `MacosDecoratedWindow` built on
Nucleus. See the [live gallery](https://nucleusframework.github.io/compose-macos-26-ui/).

## Add the dependency

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
dependencies {
    implementation("dev.nucleusframework:compose-macos-ui:<macos-ui-version>")
    // Optional: compose-macos-ui-icons-extended, compose-macos-ui-markdown
}
```

On the JVM, `compose-macos-ui` brings `nucleus-application` with it. Pick the release whose README
matches your Nucleus line.

## Open a decorated window

```kotlin
import dev.nucleusframework.application.nucleusApplication
import dev.nucleusframework.macoscompose.theme.MacosTheme
import dev.nucleusframework.macoscompose.window.MacosDecoratedWindow

fun main() = nucleusApplication {
    MacosDecoratedWindow(onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication, title = "Mail") {
        MacosTheme(darkTheme = false) { App() }
    }
}
```

Put `MacosTheme` inside the window content. The traffic lights, glass materials and window
background then follow the app theme instead of the OS appearance. On Windows and Linux the
platform window controls sit in the same title bar band.

# Jewel

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/toolkits/jewel

Style a Nucleus window with Jewel colors and metrics so the title bar and chrome match the IntelliJ Platform.

The Jewel adapter styles `DecoratedWindow` with the colors and metrics of Jewel, the JetBrains
design system, so the title bar and window chrome match the IntelliJ Platform.

## Add the dependency

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
dependencies {
    implementation("dev.nucleusframework:nucleus.nucleus-application:<version>")
    implementation("dev.nucleusframework:nucleus.decorated-window-jewel:<version>")
    // A Jewel theme, for example the standalone Int UI theme
    implementation("org.jetbrains.jewel:jewel-int-ui-standalone:<jewel-version>")
}
```

- The adapter does not expose `nucleus-application`: declare it yourself.
- Nucleus builds the adapter against Jewel `0.39.1-262.9437.29`.
- The adapter targets JDK 25: compile with `kotlin { jvmToolchain(25) }`.

## Create a Jewel window

Open a `JewelDecoratedWindow` inside a Jewel theme such as `IntUiTheme`. Without one, the window
has no colors to derive its chrome from.

```kotlin
import dev.nucleusframework.application.nucleusApplication
import dev.nucleusframework.darkmodedetector.isSystemInDarkMode
import dev.nucleusframework.window.jewel.JewelDecoratedWindow
import dev.nucleusframework.window.jewel.JewelTitleBar
import org.jetbrains.jewel.intui.standalone.theme.IntUiTheme

fun main() = nucleusApplication {
    IntUiTheme(isDark = isSystemInDarkMode()) {
        JewelDecoratedWindow(onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication, title = "Tools") {
            JewelTitleBar { /* title bar content */ }
            // Jewel widgets go here
        }
    }
}
```

Switching `isDark` flips the whole window between the light and dark IntelliJ palettes. Set
`nativePopupLayers = true` to let Jewel popups (`ListComboBox`, `PopupMenu`, `Dropdown`, tooltips)
leave the window bounds.

`JewelDecoratedWindow` and `JewelDecoratedDialog` exist only as `NucleusApplicationScope`
extensions. The AWT overload on Compose's `ApplicationScope` and the top-level dialog are gone.
See [Migrate from Nucleus 2.x](/docs/migrate/from-2.x).

## API reference

| Symbol | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `NucleusApplicationScope.JewelDecoratedWindow(...)` | The usual window parameters, plus `undecorated`, `popupFor`, `nativeContextMenu`, `hiddenFromDock`, `titleBarStyle`, `nativePopupLayers`, `transparent`, `clickThrough`, `visibleOnAllWorkspaces`, `forceX11` |
| `NucleusApplicationScope.JewelDecoratedDialog(...)` | Dialog variant |
| `DecoratedWindowScope.JewelTitleBar(...)` | Title bar slot of a window |
| `DecoratedDialogScope.JewelDialogTitleBar(...)` | Title bar slot of a dialog |
| `rememberJewelWindowStyle()` / `rememberJewelTitleBarStyle()` | Styles derived from the active Jewel theme, for your own wrapper |
| `ProvideJewelSpellcheckMenu { … }` | Jewel styling for the native context menu; the Jewel window and dialog install it |

The Jewel window has no `minimizable` or `maximizable` parameter. To drop those caption buttons,
open a `DecoratedWindow` inside `NucleusDecoratedWindowTheme` with the Jewel styles.

## What's next

- [Material 2 and 3](/docs/toolkits/material): chrome from a Compose `MaterialTheme`.
- [Windows](/docs/windows): the `DecoratedWindow` and title bar API the adapter wraps.
- [Dialogs and popups](/docs/windows/dialogs-popups): native popup layers and dialogs.

# Material 2 and 3

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/toolkits/material

Theme a Nucleus window from a Compose MaterialTheme with the Material 2 or Material 3 adapter.

The Material adapters theme a Nucleus `DecoratedWindow` from a Compose `MaterialTheme`, so the title
bar and window controls follow your app's colors.

## Add the dependency

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
dependencies {
    implementation("dev.nucleusframework:nucleus.nucleus-application:<version>")
    // Material 3
    implementation("dev.nucleusframework:nucleus.decorated-window-material3:<version>")
    implementation("org.jetbrains.compose.material3:material3:<material3-version>")
    // Or Material 2
    // implementation("dev.nucleusframework:nucleus.decorated-window-material2:<version>")
    // implementation("org.jetbrains.compose.material:material:1.12.0")
}
```

The adapters do not expose `nucleus-application`: declare it yourself.

| Adapter | Kotlin package |
| --- | --- |
| Material 3 | `dev.nucleusframework.window.material` (no `3`) |
| Material 2 | `dev.nucleusframework.window.material2` |

## Create a Material window

Call `MaterialDecoratedWindow` inside a `MaterialTheme`. `MaterialTitleBar` draws a matching title
bar.

```kotlin
import androidx.compose.material3.MaterialTheme
import androidx.compose.material3.Text
import androidx.compose.material3.lightColorScheme
import dev.nucleusframework.application.nucleusApplication
import dev.nucleusframework.window.material.MaterialDecoratedWindow
import dev.nucleusframework.window.material.MaterialTitleBar

fun main() = nucleusApplication {
    MaterialTheme(colorScheme = lightColorScheme()) {
        MaterialDecoratedWindow(onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication, title = "Material 3") {
            MaterialTitleBar { Text("Material 3") }
            Surface(Modifier.fillMaxSize()) { /* content */ }
        }
    }
}
```

For Material 2, import from `androidx.compose.material` and `dev.nucleusframework.window.material2`,
and pass `colors = lightColors()`.

The chrome follows palette switches. To follow the OS, drive the colors from
`isSystemInDarkMode()`, which comes with `nucleus-application`.

## Open a Material dialog

```kotlin
if (showAbout) {
    MaterialDecoratedDialog(onCloseRequest = { showAbout = false }, title = "About") {
        MaterialDialogTitleBar { Text("About") }
        AboutContent()
    }
}
```

Call it from `nucleusApplication { }`, like the window.

The Material windows and dialogs exist only as `NucleusApplicationScope` extensions, in both
adapters. The AWT overloads on Compose's `ApplicationScope` are gone, and the Material 2 dialog is
now a `NucleusApplicationScope` extension too. See [Migrate from Nucleus 2.x](/docs/migrate/from-2.x).

## API reference

Both adapters expose the same functions unless noted.

| Symbol | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `NucleusApplicationScope.MaterialDecoratedWindow(...)` | The usual window parameters, plus `nativePopupLayers`, `nativeContextMenu`, `hiddenFromDock`, `titleBarStyle`, `undecorated`, `transparent`, `clickThrough`, `visibleOnAllWorkspaces`, `forceX11` |
| `NucleusApplicationScope.MaterialDecoratedDialog(...)` | Dialog variant |
| `DecoratedWindowScope.MaterialTitleBar(...)` | Title bar slot of a window |
| `DecoratedDialogScope.MaterialDialogTitleBar(...)` | Title bar slot of a dialog |
| `rememberMaterialWindowStyle(colorScheme)` | Material 3 only: window style derived from a `ColorScheme` |
| `rememberMaterialTitleBarStyle(colorScheme)` | Material 3 only: title bar style; pass one to `titleBarStyle` to override the derived one |

The Material windows have no `minimizable` or `maximizable` parameter. To drop those caption
buttons, open a `DecoratedWindow` inside `NucleusDecoratedWindowTheme` with the Material styles.

## What's next

- [Toolkits](/docs/toolkits): compare Material with the native looks.
- [Jewel](/docs/toolkits/jewel): IntelliJ Platform chrome.
- [Dialogs and popups](/docs/windows/dialogs-popups): dialogs, popups, and native popup layers.

# PDF reader

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/pdf

Render PDFs, extract text, and select or copy content from Compose, with one API across Android, iOS, web, and desktop.

The PDF reader is a Kotlin Multiplatform library that renders PDF pages, extracts text, and drives selection, search, links, and thumbnails from Compose. The public API is the same on every target: you write against `PdfReaderState` and `PdfPage` once, and the library binds to the native PDF stack of each platform underneath.

The PDF reader ships from its own repository with its own release cycle, like the [system tray](/docs/os/tray). Its version number is **independent of Nucleus** — pin it separately. The artifact is `dev.nucleusframework:pdfium`, published to Maven Central.

## One API instead of one per platform

Each platform has its own PDF engine, with its own API, threading model, and coordinate conventions:

| Platform | Native PDF stack |
| -------- | ---------------- |
| Android  | `PdfRenderer` (`android.graphics.pdf`) |
| iOS      | PDFKit (`PDFView`, `PDFDocument`) |
| Web      | PDF.js |
| Desktop  | PDFBox and other JVM libraries |

Without a shared layer, a multiplatform app integrates and maintains four of these. The PDF reader replaces them with a single Compose surface backed by [PDFium](https://pdfium.googlesource.com/pdfium/) on all four, so rendering, text extraction, and selection behave identically everywhere.

## Add the dependency

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
kotlin {
    sourceSets {
        commonMain.dependencies {
            implementation("dev.nucleusframework:pdfium:<version>")
        }
    }
}
```

The `:pdfium` module uses a JVM toolchain of 17. PDFium binaries are fetched at build time from [bblanchon/pdfium-binaries](https://github.com/bblanchon/pdfium-binaries); no manual native setup is required.

## Show a PDF

Hoist a `PdfReaderState`, open the document bytes, and drop `PdfReader` into your layout:

```kotlin
import androidx.compose.foundation.layout.fillMaxSize
import androidx.compose.runtime.Composable
import androidx.compose.runtime.LaunchedEffect
import androidx.compose.ui.Modifier
import dev.nucleusframework.pdfium.PdfReader
import dev.nucleusframework.pdfium.rememberPdfReaderState

@Composable
fun HelloPdf(bytes: ByteArray) {
    val reader = rememberPdfReaderState()
    LaunchedEffect(bytes) { reader.open(bytes) }
    PdfReader(state = reader, modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize())
}
```

`PdfReader` stacks every page in a `LazyColumn`. `rememberPdfReaderState` disposes the native handles automatically when it leaves composition.

## Supported targets

| Target  | Implementation                                  |
| ------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| JVM     | JNI + Skia (Skiko)                              |
| Android | JNI (NDK `AndroidBitmap_*`)                     |
| iOS     | Kotlin/Native cinterop + Skia (Skiko)           |
| Web     | `pdfium.wasm` in a Web Worker + Skiko           |

JVM covers linux-x64/arm64, macos-x64/arm64, and win-x64/arm64. Android covers arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a, x86, and x86_64. Web covers Kotlin/WasmJS and Kotlin/JS (IR).

## How it works

`commonMain` holds the whole public API — `PdfReaderState`, `PdfPage`, `PdfThumbnail`, and `PdfReader` — over an `expect class PdfDocument`. Each source set provides the `actual`: JNI glue on JVM and Android, a Kotlin/Native cinterop on iOS, and a `pdfium.wasm` worker on the web.

Rendering uses a zero-copy path where the platform allows it. On JVM and iOS, PDFium writes pixels straight into a Skia bitmap's memory; on Android it locks the `android.graphics.Bitmap`; on the web the worker's pixel `ArrayBuffer` is written into Skia's wasm heap without an intermediate Kotlin `ByteArray`.

PDFium is single-threaded per document — it relies on FreeType's non-thread-safe `FT_Library` — so each `PdfDocument` runs on its own single-threaded dispatcher. Rendering is serialised inside a document.

## What the library covers

- Compose composables: drop `PdfReader`, `PdfPage`, or `PdfThumbnail` into any Compose UI.
- Progressive rendering (preview to full) with a debounced size flow.
- A two-tier LRU cache for reader bitmaps and thumbnails, with off-screen prefetch.
- Text extraction: per-page UTF-8 text, line-level rectangles, and per-character boxes.
- A selectable-text overlay driven by PDFium's per-character boxes.
- Clickable links: URI and internal GoTo annotations, plus URLs and e-mail addresses detected in the page text.
- Password-protected documents through `PdfError.PasswordRequired`.

PDFium is dual-licensed BSD-3-Clause / Apache-2.0, and bblanchon's binaries carry that license forward. If you ship an app built on this library, include the upstream PDFium notices.

## What's next

- [Getting started](/docs/pdf/getting-started) — load bytes, handle loading state, enable selection, links, thumbnails, and zoom.
- [API reference](/docs/pdf/api-reference) — every public type, its parameters, and defaults.
- [WebView](/docs/webview) — another Nucleus component shipped from its own repository.
- [System tray](/docs/os/tray) — tray icons and menus from a separate repository.

---

# Getting started

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/pdf/getting-started

Load PDF bytes, react to loading state, and enable text selection, links, thumbnails, and zoom.

In this tutorial, you'll open a PDF from a file picker, react to its loading state, and turn on text selection, links, a thumbnail sidebar, and zoom. Every snippet drops into a Compose Multiplatform `commonMain` source set.

## Before you start

Add the dependency described in the [PDF reader overview](/docs/pdf):

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
commonMain.dependencies {
    implementation("dev.nucleusframework:pdfium:<version>")
}
```

## Load the PDF bytes

`PdfReaderState.open` takes a `ByteArray` — how you obtain it is up to you. To pick a file with a native dialog, use [FileKit](/docs/os/file-dialogs):

```kotlin
@Composable
fun PdfPicker() {
    val reader = rememberPdfReaderState()
    val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
    val picker = rememberFilePickerLauncher(
        type = FileKitType.File(extensions = listOf("pdf")),
    ) { file ->
        if (file != null) scope.launch { reader.open(file.readBytes()) }
    }
    Column(Modifier.fillMaxSize()) {
        Button(onClick = { picker.launch() }) { Text("Open PDF…") }
        if (reader.pageCount > 0) {
            PdfReader(state = reader, modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize())
        }
    }
}
```

To load from a URL, pass the bytes from any HTTP client:

```kotlin
val client = remember { HttpClient() }
LaunchedEffect(url) { reader.open(client.get(url).readRawBytes()) }
```

## React to loading state and errors

`PdfReaderState` exposes snapshot state you can read in any composable — `isLoading`, `error`, `metadata`, and `pageCount`:

```kotlin
Box(Modifier.fillMaxSize()) {
    when {
        reader.isLoading -> CircularProgressIndicator(Modifier.align(Alignment.Center))

        reader.error is PdfError.PasswordRequired -> PasswordPrompt { password ->
            scope.launch { reader.open(bytes, password) }
        }
        reader.error is PdfError.InvalidFormat -> Text("Not a valid PDF")
        reader.error != null -> Text("Couldn't open: ${reader.error?.message}")

        reader.pageCount > 0 -> {
            Column {
                Text(reader.metadata.title ?: "Untitled")
                PdfReader(state = reader, modifier = Modifier.weight(1f))
            }
        }
    }
}
```

## Enable text selection

Set `selectableText = true` on `PdfPage`. Drag on desktop, long-press on mobile, and copy with Ctrl/Cmd+C:

```kotlin
PdfPage(
    state = reader,
    pageIndex = pageIndex,
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    selectableText = true,
)
```

Hit-testing uses PDFium's per-character boxes (`FPDFText_GetCharBox`), so selection tracks the rendered glyphs rather than Compose's own font metrics.

## Handle links

Links are enabled by default on `PdfPage` and `PdfReader`. Link annotations and URLs or e-mail addresses detected in the page text become clickable regions. External URIs open through `LocalUriHandler`; inside `PdfReader`, internal GoTo links scroll to the destination page.

Intercept clicks with `onLinkClick` — return `true` to consume the click and skip the default handling:

```kotlin
PdfReader(
    state = reader,
    onLinkClick = { link ->
        if (link.uri?.startsWith("mailto:") == true) {
            openCustomComposer(link.uri)
            true
        } else {
            false
        }
    },
)
```

## Add a thumbnail sidebar

`PdfThumbnail` renders at `RenderQuality.PREVIEW` and keeps its own LRU, so scrolling a long strip never evicts the reader's full-quality bitmaps:

```kotlin
Row(Modifier.fillMaxSize()) {
    LazyColumn(Modifier.width(160.dp).fillMaxHeight()) {
        items(reader.pageCount) { i ->
            PdfThumbnail(state = reader, pageIndex = i, modifier = Modifier.clickable { /* jumpToPage(i) */ })
        }
    }
    PdfReader(state = reader, modifier = Modifier.weight(1f).fillMaxHeight())
}
```

## Zoom and fit-to-width

`PdfReaderState.renderScale` is a plain `Float` that every `PdfPage` observes. `1.0` is fit-to-width; change it to re-render the visible pages at the new size:

```kotlin
var scale by remember { mutableStateOf(1f) }
LaunchedEffect(scale) { reader.renderScale = scale }

Slider(value = scale, onValueChange = { scale = it }, valueRange = 0.5f..3f)
```

## Extract text programmatically

`pageText` returns the Unicode of a single page; `pageTextLayout` returns line-level rectangles for search and highlighting:

```kotlin
scope.launch {
    val text = reader.pageText(pageIndex = 0)
    println(text)
}
```

The library's sample app wires a picker, sidebar, zoom, and selection into a full reader screen. See the repository's `:example` module for a complete reference.

## What's next

- [API reference](/docs/pdf/api-reference) — every public type, its parameters, and defaults.
- [PDF reader overview](/docs/pdf) — supported targets and how the render path works.
- [Native file dialogs](/docs/os/file-dialogs) — the FileKit picker used above.
