# Scheduler

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/lifecycle/background/scheduler

Run periodic, calendar, and on-boot background tasks from Kotlin that the OS fires on schedule, even when your app is closed.

The `scheduler` module runs background tasks on a schedule, even when your app is closed. You
register a task once and the OS fires it. Add
`implementation("dev.nucleusframework:nucleus.scheduler:<version>")`; it exposes
`kotlinx-serialization-json`, so apply `kotlin("plugin.serialization")` for `@Serializable` task
input.

## Schedule a task

Implement `DesktopTask`, register it under a `TaskId`, and hand scheduler launches to
`DesktopBootReceiver` at the top of `main()`:

```kotlin
val SyncId = TaskId("sync")

class SyncTask : DesktopTask {
    override suspend fun doWork(context: TaskContext): TaskResult {
        performSync()
        return TaskResult.Success
    }
}

val registry = TaskRegistry.Builder().register(SyncId) { SyncTask() }.build()

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    if (DesktopBootReceiver.isSchedulerInvocation(args)) {
        DesktopBootReceiver.handle(args = args, registry = registry)
        return
    }
    nucleusApplication(args) { /* ... */ }
}
```

Run this check before `nucleusApplication`. Otherwise each scheduled run opens a window.

Then enqueue a request. Enqueuing the same id twice is a no-op by default (see
[`TaskRequest`](#taskrequest)).

```kotlin
val scheduler = DesktopTaskScheduler.getInstance()
scheduler.enqueue(TaskRequest.periodic(SyncId, 1.hours)) // counted from enqueue time
scheduler.enqueue(TaskRequest.calendar(ReportId, CronExpression.everyDayAt(LocalTime.of(9, 0))))
scheduler.enqueue(TaskRequest.onBoot(StartupCheckId)) // at login
```

## Check the macOS sandbox

On macOS, `enqueue` returns `false` when `ExecutableRuntime.isSandboxed()` is `true`. Fall back to
[Service management](/docs/lifecycle/background/service-management):

```kotlin
if (ExecutableRuntime.isSandboxed()) {
    AppServiceManager.register(AppService.Agent("com.example.myapp.sync"))
} else {
    DesktopTaskScheduler.enqueue(TaskRequest.periodic(SyncId, 1.hours))
}
```

A Developer ID PKG (`appStore = false`) is unsandboxed and can schedule tasks; the App Store PKG
cannot. See [Executable type](/docs/lifecycle/executable-type#detect-a-sandbox).

## Notes

- `inputData` is stored as plain JSON on disk. Store a reference, not a secret.
- `CronExpression.everyHour()` fires at the top of each wall-clock hour, unlike `periodic(id, 1.hours)`.
- On macOS, an uninstall leaves the entries in place. Call `cancelAll()` from your sign-out or
  reset flow.
- To test tasks without the OS, see [Scheduler testing](/docs/lifecycle/background/scheduler-testing).

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- The OS runs your binary with `--nucleus-scheduler-run <taskId>`. The receiver loads the stored
  `TaskContext`, checks the constraints, calls `doWork`, and records the result.
- Entries: `~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.nucleusframework.<appId>.<taskId>.plist` (macOS),
  `~/.config/systemd/user/nucleus-<appId>-<taskId>.{service,timer}` (Linux),
  `\Nucleus\<appId>\<taskId>` in Task Scheduler (Windows).
- On Linux and Windows a wrapper script unregisters the task once your binary is gone.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## API reference

### DesktopTaskScheduler

`isAvailable()`, `enqueue(request)`, `cancel(taskId)`, `cancelAll()`, `isScheduled(taskId)`,
`getTaskInfo(taskId): TaskInfo?` (state, last and next run, run count, last result), and
`getAllTasks()`. `enqueue` returns `true` when scheduled or already present.

### TaskRequest

`periodic(taskId, interval)` (15 minutes minimum, shorter throws), `calendar(taskId, expression)`,
or `onBoot(taskId)`, each with an optional builder:

```kotlin
TaskRequest.periodic(SyncId, 1.hours) {
    inputData(SyncInput(endpoint = "https://api.example.com"))
    runImmediately() // also run once at registration (periodic only)
    constraints { requiredNetworkType = NetworkType.UNMETERED }
    existingTaskPolicy(ExistingTaskPolicy.REPLACE) // KEEP (default), UPDATE_DATA, REPLACE
}
```

`retryPolicy(RetryPolicy.Linear | ExponentialBackoff)` is stored but not applied yet.

`CronExpression`: `everyDayAt(time)`, `everyWeekdayAt(time)` (Monday to Friday),
`everyWeekdayAt(day, time)`, `everyHour()`.

`TaskResult`: `Success`, `Failure(message)` (no retry), `Retry(message)` (one re-run about
5 minutes later).

### Constraints

Checked when the task fires. An unmet periodic run waits for the next trigger; an unmet calendar
or on-boot run retries once about 5 minutes later.

| Property | Description |
|---|---|
| `requiredNetworkType` | `NOT_REQUIRED`, `CONNECTED`, or `UNMETERED`. |
| `requiresBatteryNotLow` | Battery above 15 %. No battery passes. |
| `requiresCharging` | Plugged in. |
| `requiresDeviceIdle` | No user input for at least 5 minutes. |
| `minimumStorageBytes` | Minimum free space on the app partition. |

### SchedulerConfig

If your app starts through a custom launcher, point the scheduler at it before the first
`enqueue`. A later change only affects tasks enqueued afterwards.

```kotlin
SchedulerConfig.executablePath = "/opt/myapp/myapp-launcher" // absolute; null = current executable
SchedulerConfig.executableArguments = listOf("--background") // before --nucleus-scheduler-run
```

## What's next

- [Scheduler testing](/docs/lifecycle/background/scheduler-testing): run tasks in memory with virtual time.
- [Service management](/docs/lifecycle/background/service-management): background agents for sandboxed macOS builds.
- [System info](/docs/os/system-info): the signals behind the constraints.
- [Auto-launch](/docs/lifecycle/background/launch-at-login): start the app itself at login.

# Scheduler testing

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/lifecycle/background/scheduler-testing

Test doubles for the scheduler that run background tasks in memory, with virtual time and controllable constraints.

`scheduler-testing` runs your [scheduler](/docs/lifecycle/background/scheduler) tasks in memory, with a
virtual clock and simulated constraints. Add
`testImplementation("dev.nucleusframework:nucleus.scheduler-testing:<version>")`; it brings
`scheduler` with it.

## Test a task in isolation

`TestTaskRunner.runTask()` calls `doWork()` with a fabricated `TaskContext` and returns the
`TaskResult`:

```kotlin
@Test
fun `sync succeeds`() = runTest {
    val result = TestTaskRunner.runTask(
        task = SyncTask(),
        taskId = TaskId("sync"),
        inputData = TaskData.of(SyncInput(endpoint = "https://test.api")),
    )
    assertEquals(TaskResult.Success, result)
}
```

`taskId`, `inputData`, and `runAttemptCount` are optional. Set `runAttemptCount` to exercise retry
logic.

## Run tasks through the scheduler

`TestDesktopTaskScheduler` replaces the backend behind `DesktopTaskScheduler`. Wrap it in
`use { }` so the real backend comes back after the test:

```kotlin
TestDesktopTaskScheduler().use { testScheduler ->
    testScheduler.install()
    DesktopTaskScheduler.enqueue(TaskRequest.periodic(SyncId, 2.hours))

    // Six virtual hours: the 2-hour task fires three times.
    val fired = testScheduler.advanceTimeBy(6.hours, registry)
    assertEquals(3, fired.size)
    assertEquals(LastTaskResult.Success, testScheduler.getExecutionHistory(SyncId).last().result)
}
```

`advanceTimeBy()` fires periodic tasks only. Run a calendar or on-boot task with
`runTask(taskId, registry)`.

## Simulate constraints

Pass a `TestConstraintChecker` to the test scheduler so both install and uninstall together:

```kotlin
val checker = TestConstraintChecker()
TestDesktopTaskScheduler(constraintChecker = checker).use { testScheduler ->
    testScheduler.install()
    checker.networkConnected = false

    // A task that needs the network is recorded as ConstraintsNotMet.
    assertNull(testScheduler.runTask(SyncId, registry))
}
```

## API reference

### TestDesktopTaskScheduler

`TestDesktopTaskScheduler(constraintChecker: TestConstraintChecker? = null)`, `Closeable`.

| Member | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `install()` / `uninstall()` | Routes `DesktopTaskScheduler` to this instance, or restores the platform backend. `close()` uninstalls. |
| `runTask(taskId, registry)` | Runs one enqueued task now. `null` when its constraints fail; throws if the task is not enqueued. |
| `advanceTimeBy(duration, registry)` | Advances virtual time and returns the `ExecutionRecord`s of the periodic tasks it fired. |
| `currentVirtualTimeMs` | Current virtual time. |
| `getExecutionHistory(taskId)` / `getAllExecutionHistory()` | Run history, oldest first. |
| `getEnqueuedRequest(taskId)` / `getEnqueuedRequests()` | Stored requests. |

`ExecutionRecord` holds `taskId`, `result: LastTaskResult`, `runAttemptCount`, and `virtualTimeMs`.

### TestConstraintChecker

`Closeable`, with `install()` and `uninstall()` for standalone use.

| Field | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `networkConnected` | `true` | A network is active. |
| `networkUnmetered` | `true` | The active network is unmetered. |
| `batteryLevel` | `1.0f` | `0.0` to `1.0`; `null` means no battery. |
| `isCharging` | `false` | Plugged in. |
| `idleTimeSeconds` | `0L` | User idle time; `-1` means unavailable. |
| `availableStorageBytes` | `Long.MAX_VALUE` | Free disk space. |

- [Scheduler](/docs/lifecycle/background/scheduler): tasks, requests, constraints, and retries.
- [Lifecycle overview](/docs/lifecycle): the other lifecycle modules.

# Service management (macOS)

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/lifecycle/background/service-management

Register login items, launch agents, and launch daemons through the macOS SMAppService API from Kotlin.

`service-management-macos` registers login items, launch agents, and launch daemons on macOS 13+.
The plists are embedded in the bundle at build time, so the services also work in the Mac App
Store sandbox. Add `implementation("dev.nucleusframework:nucleus.service-management-macos:<version>")`
and check `AppServiceManager.isAvailable` before you register a service.

## Launch the app at login

```kotlin
AppServiceManager.register(AppService.MainApp)

when (AppServiceManager.status(AppService.MainApp)) {
    AppServiceStatus.ENABLED -> { /* launches at next login */ }
    AppServiceStatus.REQUIRES_APPROVAL -> AppServiceManager.openSystemSettingsLoginItems()
    else -> {}
}
```

For launch at login on every OS, use [`AutoLaunch`](/docs/lifecycle/background/launch-at-login). Use this module
directly for agents and daemons.

## Register a background agent

A launch agent runs in the user session on a schedule, independent of your windows.

1. Declare the agent:

   ```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
   nucleus.application {
       nativeDistributions {
           macOS {
               launchAgents {
                   agent("com.example.myapp.sync") {
                       arguments("--sync")
                       startInterval(900) // 15 minutes
                   }
               }
           }
       }
   }
   ```

2. Handle the argument in `main()`, before `nucleusApplication`:

   ```kotlin
   fun main(args: Array<String>) {
       if ("--sync" in args) {
           performSync()
           return
       }
       nucleusApplication(args) { /* ... */ }
   }
   ```

3. Register it from your app with the same label:

   ```kotlin
   AppServiceManager.register(AppService.Agent("com.example.myapp.sync"))
   ```

The first registration shows a system notification. The user approves it there, or later in
System Settings → General → Login Items.

To fire at wall-clock times, call `calendar { }` once per moment. Weekdays follow launchd: 0 is
Sunday, 1 is Monday.

```kotlin
agent("com.example.myapp.weekly-cleanup") {
    arguments("--cleanup")
    calendar { weekday = 1; hour = 18; minute = 0 } // Monday 18:00
    calendar { weekday = 5; hour = 18; minute = 0 } // Friday 18:00
}
```

Unlike the [scheduler](/docs/lifecycle/background/scheduler), agents have no constraints or input data, and
the set is fixed at build time. Branch on `ExecutableRuntime.isSandboxed()` to pick one.

With ProGuard, keep `-keep class dev.nucleusframework.servicemanagement.** { *; }`.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- The module wraps Apple's `SMAppService`. `AppService.MainApp` maps to `SMAppService.mainApp` and
  needs no plist.
- Each agent plist lands in `Contents/Library/LaunchAgents/<label>.plist`. Deleting the app
  removes its services.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## API reference

### AppServiceManager

| Member | Returns | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `isAvailable` | `Boolean` | `true` on macOS 13+ with the native library loaded. |
| `register(service)` | `Result<Unit>` | Registers the service so it can run. |
| `unregister(service, callback = {})` | `Unit` | Asynchronous. `callback` receives an error message, or `null` on success. |
| `status(service)` | `AppServiceStatus` | `NOT_REGISTERED`, `ENABLED`, `REQUIRES_APPROVAL`, or `NOT_FOUND`. |
| `openSystemSettingsLoginItems()` | `Boolean` | Opens the Login Items pane. |

### AppService

| Variant | Use |
|---|---|
| `MainApp` | The app itself as a login item. |
| `LoginItem(bundleIdentifier)` | A helper app in `Contents/Library/LoginItems/`. |
| `Agent(label)` | A launch agent in `Contents/Library/LaunchAgents/`. |
| `Daemon(label)` | A launch daemon in `Contents/Library/LaunchDaemons/`. |

### `launchAgents { agent(label) { ... } }`

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| `bundleProgram(path)` | Executable inside the bundle. Defaults to the one named after `packageName`. |
| `arguments(vararg)` | Arguments passed to the program. |
| `startInterval(seconds)` | Fixed interval; 900 (15 minutes) is the recommended minimum. |
| `calendar { ... }` | Wall-clock trigger with `month`, `day`, `weekday`, `hour`, `minute`. Repeatable. |
| `runAtLoad(enabled = true)` | Run as soon as launchd loads the agent. |
| `keepAlive(enabled = true)` | Restart the agent when it exits. |
| `processType(type)` | `"Background"` (default), `"Standard"`, or `"Adaptive"`. |

## What's next

- [Auto-launch](/docs/lifecycle/background/launch-at-login): launch at login on every OS.
- [Scheduler](/docs/lifecycle/background/scheduler): dynamic background tasks with constraints.
- [Packaging for macOS](/docs/packaging/macos): sign and distribute the bundle.

# Runtimes and performance

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/performance

Build the same Kotlin source as a GraalVM native image or as a JDK image with an AOT cache, pick the right one, and detect the runtime from code.

Nucleus builds one Kotlin source tree into two runtimes: a GraalVM native image, or a JDK image
with an ahead-of-time (AOT) cache. You pick the runtime in `build.gradle.kts`, and your code stays
the same.

## Compare the runtimes

|                    | GraalVM Native Image              | JDK + AOT cache                           |
|--------------------|-----------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| Starts and runs    | Fast start, less memory           | Faster once HotSpot compiles hot paths    |
| Dynamic features   | Declared at build time            | Reflection, class loading, agents, JFR    |
| Minimum JDK        | GraalVM 25, provisioned for you   | JDK 25 for the AOT cache                  |
| Fits               | Tray and menu-bar apps, utilities, launchers, store builds | IDE-like tools, CPU-heavy work, plugin hosts, scripting engines |

Both can live in one project: ship a native image to a store and a JDK build for direct download.

## Switch between runtimes

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
nucleus.application {
    mainClass = "com.example.MainKt"

    // GraalVM native image
    graalvm {
        isEnabled = true
        imageName = "myapp"
    }

    // JDK image with an AOT cache
    nativeDistributions {
        enableAotCache = true
    }
}
```

The JVM tasks (`packageDistributionForCurrentOS`, …) produce the JDK image, and the GraalVM tasks
(`packageGraalvmNativeDistributionForCurrentOS`, …) produce the native one. On the JVM path, add
`nucleusOptimization = true` for a faster cold start: see [Startup optimization](/docs/performance/startup).

## Detect the runtime at run time

```kotlin
import dev.nucleusframework.aot.runtime.AotRuntime
import dev.nucleusframework.aot.runtime.AotRuntimeMode
import dev.nucleusframework.core.runtime.ExecutableRuntime

when (AotRuntime.mode()) {
    AotRuntimeMode.TRAINING -> { /* AOT training run: skip user-facing work */ }
    AotRuntimeMode.RUNTIME -> { /* launched with an AOT cache */ }
    AotRuntimeMode.OFF -> { /* plain JVM or native image */ }
}

val isNative: Boolean = ExecutableRuntime.isGraalVmNativeImage
```

`ExecutableRuntime.type()` returns the package format (`DMG`, `MSI`, `DEB`, `DEV` and others). See
[Executable type](/docs/lifecycle/executable-type).

## What's next

- [GraalVM Native Image](/docs/performance/graalvm): toolchain, DSL, metadata and CI.
- [AOT cache](/docs/performance/aot-cache): training runs and the cache lifecycle.
- [Startup optimization](/docs/performance/startup): the `nucleusOptimization` knobs, idle GC and `lastJdk`.
- [Benchmarks](/docs/performance/benchmarks): CPU, rendering and list-load results on the JVM, a native image and other toolkits.
- [Native code in Kotlin](/docs/performance/native-code), [Native library loader](/docs/performance/native-library-loader),
  [Native HTTP](/docs/performance/native-http) and [Native SSL](/docs/performance/native-ssl): native interop modules.

# Startup optimization

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/performance/startup

Turn on the nucleusOptimization pack to shorten JVM startup and lower idle memory, and package the app with the current OpenJDK through lastJdk.

`nucleusOptimization` is a set of JVM packaging defaults tuned for desktop apps. It is off by
default, and your source code stays the same when you turn it on.

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
nucleus.application {
    nucleusOptimization = true
    nucleusOptimization { idleGc = false } // optional: force one knob on or off
}
```

Each knob is a `Boolean?`: `null` follows the master switch, `true` or `false` forces it. You can
also leave the pack off and turn on a single knob.

## Knobs

| Knob | Effect when on |
|------|----------------|
| `serialGc` | Uses the Serial collector when `garbageCollector` is unset. |
| `compactHeap` | Adds `-Xms32m` and `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=25`, each one only if `jvmArgs` does not already set it. |
| `singleJar` | Flattens the runtime JARs into one JAR. With ProGuard, it sets `joinOutputJars` instead. |
| `idleGc` | Collects garbage while the app sits unused. See [Idle GC](#idle-gc). |
| `lastJdk` | Packages and runs the app with OpenJDK 27. See [Package with the latest JDK](#package-with-the-latest-jdk). |

The pack never replaces a value you set (`garbageCollector`, `javaHome`, `-Xms`,
`-XX:MaxRAMPercentage`), and it does not enable the [AOT cache](/docs/performance/aot-cache) or
ProGuard. In a GraalVM native image only `idleGc` applies.

## Package with the latest JDK

With `lastJdk` on, the plugin downloads OpenJDK 27 GA (BellSoft Liberica JDK 27 on Intel macOS
and Windows on ARM) the first time a packaging or `run` task needs it. The app ships with that
runtime; your `jvmToolchain(...)` stays as it is.

- Set `NUCLEUS_JDK_HOME` to a local JDK 27 to skip the download.
- An explicit `javaHome` disables `lastJdk`.

## Idle GC

Idle GC runs `System.gc()` right away when a window is minimized, or 3 s after every window has
lost focus. Startup never triggers one. It covers the windows `nucleusApplication` opens and works
in native images too. Pass `-Dnucleus.optimization.idleGc=false` to turn it off for one run.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- `serialGc` and `compactHeap` also apply to the `run` task.
- `lastJdk` pins build 35 from [jdk.java.net/27](https://jdk.java.net/27/) and caches it under
  `<gradle-user-home>/nucleus/jdk`. The fallback uses the full Liberica JDK, since Lite has no
  `jmods` for `jlink`. A `NUCLEUS_JDK_HOME` that is not JDK 27 or has no `bin/java` is ignored
  with a warning.
- A native image reads idle GC from `nucleus/nucleus-app.properties`, since it has no launcher `.cfg`.
- A native image takes its collector and heap from `graalvm { garbageCollector; maxHeapSizePercent }`.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## What's next

- [AOT cache](/docs/performance/aot-cache): skip JVM warmup with a Project Leyden cache.
- [GraalVM Native Image](/docs/performance/graalvm): compile the app to a native binary.
- [Gradle DSL reference](/docs/reference/gradle-dsl): every property of `nucleus.application`.

# Benchmarks

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/performance/benchmarks

Measured results of one CPU, rendering and list-load suite run inside a Compose desktop app on the JVM, GraalVM Native Image, SwiftUI, Tauri and Flutter.

The [`benchmark-demo`](https://github.com/NucleusFramework/Nucleus/tree/main/examples/benchmark-demo)
example runs one suite inside a Compose desktop app: 13 CPU kernels, three rendering ramps and a
list-load test. The same kernels are ported to SwiftUI, Tauri and Flutter. Every variant ran on an
Apple M4 on 2026-07-16.

Higher is better for CPU and GFX; lower is better for list, peak RAM and app size. Composite
scores compare only within this suite.

## Summary

Sorted by composite CPU score.

| # | Variant | Runtime | CPU | GFX | list (ms) | Peak RAM | App size |
|---|---------|---------|----:|----:|----------:|---------:|---------:|
| 1 | **jvm-graal** | GraalVM 25.0.3 JIT + ProGuard | 146.7 | 13041 | 21.0 | 695 MB | 160 MB |
| 2 | **tauri** | Rust + WebView (WKWebView) | 142.2 | 15013 | 233.0 | 794 MB † | 5.6 MB ‡ |
| 3 | **jvm-c2-pg** | OpenJDK 26 C2 + ProGuard | 140.4 | 13041 | 20.9 | 616 MB | 119 MB |
| 4 | **swiftui** | Swift/LLVM + SwiftUI | 138.7 | 15254 | 14.4 | 268 MB | 0.34 MB ‡ |
| 5 | **jvm-c2** | OpenJDK 26 C2 (no ProGuard) | 138.5 | 13041 | 21.6 | 620 MB | 136 MB |
| 6 | **aot-o3-pgo** | GraalVM Native `-O3` + PGO | 132.7 | 13859 | 17.1 | 269 MB | 129 MB |
| 7 | **aot-o3** | GraalVM Native `-O3` (ML-inferred) | 100.8 | 13859 | 17.1 | 297 MB | 174 MB |
| 8 | **aot-o2** | GraalVM Native `-O2` | 86.9 | 11239 | 17.2 | 278 MB | 150 MB |
| 9 | **aot-os** | GraalVM Native size-opt (`-Os`) | 80.1 | 10433 | 17.3 | 326 MB | 129 MB |
| 10 | **flutter** | Dart AOT + Impeller | 57.3 | 15133 | 17.2 | 196 MB | 37 MB |

† Includes the WebKit processes; an upper bound. ‡ Excludes the system engine (SwiftUI and AppKit,
or WebKit), so it does not compare directly with the variants that ship their runtime.

## Read the results

- **CPU.** GraalVM JIT scores highest (146.7). Tauri (142), SwiftUI (139) and OpenJDK C2 (138 to
  140) sit close together. GraalVM Native reaches that group only with PGO (100.8 to 132.7).
- **PGO.** `aot-o3-pgo` reaches 132.7 CPU with 269 MB of peak RAM, against 616 to 695 MB for the
  JVM variants. The cost is the PGO workflow: an instrumented build, a GUI run, then a rebuild.
  The profile also shrinks the image from 174 MB to 129 MB.
- **RAM.** Flutter uses the least (196 MB), then SwiftUI (268) and GraalVM Native (269 to 326).
  The JVM variants use 616 to 695 MB, and Tauri 794 MB (†).
- **List load.** GraalVM Native takes about 17 ms, the JVM about 21 ms, SwiftUI 14 ms and Tauri
  233 ms.
- **Flutter** has the lowest CPU score (57.3) but one of the highest GFX scores (15133).

## Per-kernel CPU

Throughput, higher is better.

| Kernel | jvm-graal | tauri | jvm-c2-pg | swiftui | jvm-c2 | aot-o3-pgo | aot-o3 | aot-o2 | aot-os | flutter |
|--------|----:|----:|----:|----:|----:|----:|----:|----:|----:|----:|
| mandelbrot | 4.09 | 4.13 | 4.33 | 3.92 | 3.99 | 1.98 | 3.32 | 1.97 | 3.27 | 3.61 |
| nbody | 700.6 | 693.2 | 639.6 | 659.4 | 691.3 | 694.7 | 683.0 | 654.8 | 678.3 | 608.7 |
| raytracer | 17.2 | 19.8 | 18.9 | 19.8 | 19.0 | 17.5 | 15.8 | 14.0 | 7.0 | 4.2 |
| matmul | 14217 | 16224 | 16690 | 16215 | 16724 | 12225 | 3877 | 3244 | 3105 | 3054 |
| blur | 93.4 | 44.5 | 59.7 | 80.7 | 49.2 | 91.5 | 49.5 | 46.6 | 36.5 | 30.0 |
| sha256 | 332.9 | 442.1 | 361.2 | 360.3 | 361.7 | 326.9 | 296.8 | 294.9 | 268.2 | 192.4 |
| sieve | 708.5 | 642.3 | 565.9 | 603.6 | 599.9 | 725.9 | 467.2 | 463.2 | 484.4 | 268.6 |
| fft | 407.8 | 452.7 | 441.5 | 436.9 | 441.1 | 363.9 | 369.6 | 376.3 | 356.8 | 366.9 |
| pi | 0.09 | 0.11 | 0.11 | 0.11 | 0.10 | 0.10 | 0.09 | 0.09 | 0.09 | 0.08 |
| mandelbrot_mt | 15.5 | 16.5 | 15.6 | 16.1 | 16.1 | 14.5 | 14.1 | 7.5 | 12.2 | 10.6 |
| raytracer_mt | 74.5 | 81.2 | 68.6 | 75.0 | 67.2 | 71.4 | 60.2 | 49.9 | 25.5 | 13.7 |
| matmul_mt | 62088 | 69442 | 64038 | 33013 | 63925 | 60113 | 19988 | 17255 | 15956 | 9731 |
| blur_mt | 345.0 | 188.4 | 244.1 | 261.7 | 238.3 | 285.9 | 203.5 | 194.4 | 155.1 | 40.0 |

## Render ramps

Highest load sustained at 55 fps or more, higher is better.

| Variant | Particles | Stars | Texts |
|---------|----:|----:|----:|
| swiftui | 125000 | 18175 | 3906 |
| aot-o3 / o3-pgo | 75000 | 14540 | 6102 |
| jvm (×3) | 50000 | 18175 | 6102 |
| flutter | 50000 | 18175 | 9533 |
| aot-o2 | 50000 | 11632 | 6102 |
| aot-os | 50000 | 9306 | 6102 |
| tauri | 25000 | 18175 | 18618 |

## Reproduce

```shell title="terminal"
cd examples/benchmark-demo

# JVM and native matrix
JAVA_HOME=<jbr-21> GRAALVM_HOME=<graalvm-25> JDK_C2_HOME=<jdk-26> \
  ONLY="jvm-c2 jvm-c2-pg jvm-graal aot-os aot-o2 aot-o3 aot-o3-pgo" ./run-all.sh

# Ports
ONLY="swiftui tauri flutter" ./run-all.sh
```

Run the native builds with `JAVA_HOME` pointing at GraalVM, or Gradle may pick a cached Oracle
JDK 25 without `native-image` and the compile fails. Each variant writes a result JSON, and the
example's `RESULTS.md` holds the full per-variant appendix.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- **Setup:** Apple M4, 10 cores, on AC power. Oracle GraalVM 25.1.3+9.1 (Java 25.0.3), OpenJDK
  26.0.1, Gradle daemon on JBR 21.
- **Protocol:** 3 discarded warmups, then the best of 5 over the CPU kernels. Variants run one at
  a time in one session, peak RSS is sampled during each run, and every self-check passes.
- **Tauri (†):** the Tauri process alone has a 177 MB RSS. The 794 MB sums the WebKit processes
  (`WebContent`, `GPU`, `Networking`) and counts shared `WebKit.framework` pages more than once.
  Its list goes through the DOM and a canvas.
- **Kernels:** without PGO, `matmul` drops to 3877 MFLOP/s against 12225 with it. Graal does well
  on `blur` and `sieve`, less well on `fft` and `sha256`, and PGO regresses `mandelbrot` (1.98
  against 3.32).
- **Reproduce:** Gradle picks the wrong JDK because a cached Oracle JDK 25 matches the
  `vendor=ORACLE`, `version=25` toolchain spec.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

- [GraalVM Native Image](/docs/performance/graalvm): what a native image changes for a Nucleus app.

- [AOT cache](/docs/performance/aot-cache): faster startup on the JVM path.

# GraalVM Native Image

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/performance/graalvm

Compile a Nucleus app ahead of time into a self-contained native binary. The plugin provisions GraalVM and generates the reachability metadata for you.

GraalVM Native Image compiles a Compose Desktop app into one binary that runs without a JVM. The
Nucleus plugin downloads GraalVM and generates the reflection metadata, so the source that builds
your JVM app also builds the native image.

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
nucleus.application {
    mainClass = "com.example.MainKt"
    graalvm {
        isEnabled = true
        imageName = "myapp"
    }
}
```

Run it with `./gradlew runGraalvmNative`. See [Tasks and CI](/docs/performance/graalvm/tasks-ci)
for packaging.

## Know the limits

[Runtimes and performance](/docs/performance#compare-the-runtimes) helps you choose between a
native image and the JDK build. On the native side:

- **Closed world.** No `Class.forName` on values computed at run time, no custom class loaders,
  no scripting engines, no bytecode generation. Spring, Groovy, ByteBuddy mocking and heavy JNA
  use do not fit.
- **No JIT.** Sustained CPU-heavy work runs slower than on HotSpot. Oracle GraalVM's PGO closes
  most of the gap.
- **One build per OS.** You compile on each target OS, so a release needs a CI matrix.

Ktor, kotlinx.serialization, Coil, SQLite, Jewel, Compose and SLF4J work without extra
configuration. For a daemon or a CLI, see
[Build a headless image](/docs/performance/graalvm/configuration#build-a-headless-image).

## Requirements

| Platform | Required |
|----------|----------|
| **macOS** | Xcode Command Line Tools |
| **Windows** | MSVC (Visual Studio Build Tools) |
| **Linux** | GCC, `patchelf`, and `xvfb` for headless builds |

The plugin downloads GraalVM Community Edition (25.4 by default) on the first native build. CE is
GPLv2 with the Classpath Exception, so you can ship it inside a paid app. See
[Provision the toolchain](/docs/performance/graalvm/configuration#provision-the-toolchain) to pick
another version or Oracle GraalVM.

If your `main()` does not go through `nucleusApplication`, add `nucleus.graalvm-runtime` and call
`GraalVmInitializer.initialize()` before any AWT or Compose code runs.

## What's next

- [Configuration](/docs/performance/graalvm/configuration): the `graalvm { }` DSL, toolchain, garbage collector and PGO.
- [Automatic metadata](/docs/performance/graalvm/automatic-metadata): what the plugin registers and how to fill gaps.
- [Tasks and CI](/docs/performance/graalvm/tasks-ci): Gradle tasks, output layout and a GitHub Actions matrix.

---

# Configuration

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/performance/graalvm/configuration

Reference for the graalvm { } block that configures native-image builds, including the toolchain, garbage collector, build arguments, PGO, the metadata repository, and per-OS settings.

The `graalvm { }` block inside `nucleus.application { }` configures native-image builds. Set
`isEnabled = true` and the plugin provisions everything else:

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
nucleus.application {
    mainClass = "com.example.MainKt"
    graalvm {
        isEnabled = true
        imageName = "myapp"
        optimization = NativeImageOptimization.SIZE // optional, default -O2
    }
}
```

## Build a headless image

For a daemon or a CLI, set `headless = true`. The image leaves out AWT, Java2D, Skiko and Compose
and runs with `-Djava.awt.headless=true`. Keep `false` for any app with a window or a tray icon.

## Provision the toolchain

The plugin downloads **GraalVM Community Edition** into `<gradle-user-home>/nucleus/graalvm` on the
first native-image task. A `GRAALVM_HOME` that matches the requested distribution wins.

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
graalvm {
    toolchain {
        distribution = GraalvmDistribution.COMMUNITY // default, or ORACLE
        channel = GraalvmChannel.INNOVATION          // default 25i4; LTS gives 25
        // version = "25.0.1"                        // overrides channel
    }
}
```

- `autoDownload = false` resolves through Gradle toolchains (`javaLanguageVersion`, `jvmVendor`)
  instead. Use it, or `GRAALVM_HOME`, for Liberica NIK or Mandrel.
- Intel Macs get BellSoft Liberica NIK 25.0.x (`macosIntelFallback`), since GraalVM stopped
  shipping Intel macOS after 25.0.1.
- Floating versions (`"25"`, `"25i4"`) stick once downloaded. Delete their folder under
  `installDir` to update.

### Roll back to GraalVM 25.3

If a build regresses on the default `25i4`, set `toolchain { version = "25i3" }`.

### Choose a distribution

Oracle GraalVM adds Profile-Guided Optimization, `-O3`, ML-inferred profiles,
`advancedObfuscation` and the G1 collector. On Community Edition the build skips those with a
warning.

The [GraalVM Free Terms and Conditions](https://www.oracle.com/downloads/licenses/graal-free-license.html)
allow commercial use but forbid charging "any fees associated with such distribution or use".
Nucleus ships GraalVM runtime libraries inside your app bundle, so the clause applies to it.

## Choose a garbage collector

A native image fixes its collector at build time. Serial, the default, fits desktop heaps. Pick G1
once the heap passes roughly 1 to 2 GB.

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
nucleus.application {
    garbageCollector = GarbageCollector.Z                  // JVM distribution and run task
    graalvm {
        garbageCollector = NativeImageGarbageCollector.G1  // baked into the image
    }
}
```

| `NativeImageGarbageCollector` | Availability |
|-------------------------------|--------------|
| `SERIAL` | Every toolchain. The default. |
| `G1` | Oracle GraalVM only. Linux from 25.0; Windows and macOS from 25.4. Falls back to Serial with a warning elsewhere. |
| `EPSILON` | Never reclaims memory. Benchmarks and short-lived processes only. |

An explicit `-XX:+Use…GC` in `jvmArgs` wins over the JVM-side `garbageCollector`. The
[startup pack](/docs/performance/startup) also turns on [idle GC](/docs/performance/startup#idle-gc)
in the native image.

## Catch missing registrations in the dev loop

`runGraalvmNative` runs with `--exact-reachability-metadata` for the packages in
`exactReachabilityMetadata`. An unregistered lookup there throws
`MissingReflectionRegistrationError` naming the missing element. Distributable and packaging tasks
never get the flag.

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
graalvm {
    exactReachabilityMetadata = ExactReachabilityMetadata.APP_PACKAGES // default: mainClass package
    // ExactReachabilityMetadata.packages("com.example", "com.example.shared")
    // ExactReachabilityMetadata.OFF
}
```

Pass `-Pnucleus.graalvm.missingRegistration=warn|exit|throw` (default `warn`) to list every missing
registration in one run.

## Set build arguments

`buildArgs` go to `native-image` as is and win over the typed properties. Use them for flags with
no property, such as `-H:-IncludeMethodData` (saves several MB). Nucleus initializes SLF4J at run
time; to move it to build time with a fixed backend, add
`buildArgs.add("--initialize-at-build-time=org.slf4j")`.

## Optimize with a PGO profile

Profile-Guided Optimization needs Oracle GraalVM.

1. Run `./gradlew runWithPgoInstrument`, exercise the hot paths, then quit. The profile lands in
   `pgo { profile }` (default `graalvm/pgo/default.iprof`).
2. Commit the `.iprof` file. Full builds and packaging tasks apply it; `runGraalvmNative` does not.

Pass `-Pnucleus.graalvm.pgo=off` to build once without it, or set `pgo { enabled = false }`.

## Configure the metadata repository

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
graalvm {
    metadataRepository {
        // enabled = true, version = "1.1.4" by default
        moduleToConfigVersion.put("io.ktor:ktor-client-core", "3.0.0")
        excludedModules.add("com.example:noisy-lib")
    }
}
```

## Configure macOS and Windows

- `macOS { minimumSystemVersion }` defaults to `"12.0"`. `macOsSdkVersion` defaults to `"26.0"`;
  Liquid Glass needs SDK 26. `cStubsSrc` links extra C stubs.
- On Windows the plugin copies `vcruntime140.dll`, `vcruntime140_1.dll` and `msvcp140.dll` next to
  the `.exe`, so the app needs no Visual C++ Redistributable. Tune it with
  `windows { bundleCRuntime; dlls; sourceDir }`.

## No release variant

There is no `packageReleaseGraalvmNative`. `native-image` already removes dead code, and ProGuard
could rename classes the metadata references. Use `NativeImageOptimization.SIZE` to shrink.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- A headless build skips the platform metadata and the GUI packs (`jdk-awt`, `jdk-fonts`,
  `jdk-graphics2d`, Skiko, Compose, tray, media player, webview) and copies no GUI libraries.
- Install folders carry the distribution name (`graalvm-community-jdk-*`, `graalvm-jdk-*`). A
  `GRAALVM_HOME` of the other distribution is ignored with a warning.
- The plugin reads `GRAALVM_VERSION` from the toolchain's `release` file to decide on G1. GraalVM
  25.3 fails to link G1 on Windows and macOS (`g1gc-cr.lib`).
- `maxHeapSizePercent` becomes `-R:MaximumHeapSizePercent` (Serial, Epsilon) or
  `-R:MaxRAMPercentage` (G1).
- Before JDK 23, exact reachability falls back to `-H:ThrowMissingRegistrationErrors=` or is
  skipped.
- On Linux and macOS the plugin strips the executable, which saves tens of MB.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## graalvm { } reference

| Property | Default | Notes |
|----------|---------|-------|
| `isEnabled` | `false` | Master switch. |
| `headless` | `false` | See [Build a headless image](#build-a-headless-image). |
| `imageName` | package name | Output binary name. |
| `march` | per platform | `NATIVE` targets the build CPU, `COMPATIBILITY` older CPUs. Unset means `COMPATIBILITY`, except `NATIVE` on Apple Silicon. |
| `optimization` | `-O2` | `QUICK_BUILD` (`-Ob`), `NONE`, `LEVEL_1`, `LEVEL_2`, `LEVEL_3` (Oracle), `SIZE` (`-Os`). |
| `allCharsets` | `false` | Adds `-H:+AddAllCharsets`. Legacy encodings only. |
| `mlProfileInference` | `true` | `false` adds `-H:-MLProfileInference`. Oracle only. |
| `advancedObfuscation` | `false` | Adds `-H:AdvancedObfuscation=`. Oracle only. |
| `autoIncludeResources` | `true` | Bundle resources of the project and its `project(...)` dependencies. |
| `maxHeapSizePercent` | `25` | Default max heap as a percent of RAM. |
| `maxHeapSize` | unset | Absolute max heap (`"2g"`). Wins over the percent. |
| `garbageCollector` | Serial | See [Choose a garbage collector](#choose-a-garbage-collector). |
| `exactReachabilityMetadata` | `APP_PACKAGES` | `runGraalvmNative` only. See [above](#catch-missing-registrations-in-the-dev-loop). |
| `detectOrphanProjectClasses` | `true` | See [Automatic metadata](/docs/performance/graalvm/automatic-metadata#detect-orphan-project-classes). |
| `reflectionForProjectClasses` | `false` | Registers every project class with a public no-arg constructor. Grows the image. |
| `buildArgs` | empty | Appended verbatim. |
| `javaLanguageVersion`, `jvmVendor` | `25`, unset | With `toolchain { autoDownload = false }` only. |
| `nativeImageConfigBaseDir` | unset | Folder of your own `reachability-metadata.json`. |
| `toolchain { }` | auto-download | See [Provision the toolchain](#provision-the-toolchain). |
| `pgo { }` | enabled | See [Optimize with a PGO profile](#optimize-with-a-pgo-profile). |
| `metadataRepository { }` | enabled | See [Configure the metadata repository](#configure-the-metadata-repository). |
| `macOS { }`, `windows { }` | | See [Configure macOS and Windows](#configure-macos-and-windows). |

## What's next

- [Automatic metadata](/docs/performance/graalvm/automatic-metadata): what the plugin registers and how to fill gaps.
- [Tasks and CI](/docs/performance/graalvm/tasks-ci): Gradle tasks and a CI matrix.
- [Gradle DSL reference](/docs/reference/gradle-dsl): the full `nucleus { }` surface.

# Automatic metadata

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/performance/graalvm/automatic-metadata

The Nucleus plugin generates GraalVM reachability metadata at build time. Fill the gaps with the tracing agent and prune your own entries.

The Nucleus plugin generates the reflection, resource and JNI metadata that `native-image` needs,
so a native build works without a hand-written `reachability-metadata.json`. It covers Compose,
Ktor, kotlinx.serialization, SQLite, Coil and the JDK, your other dependencies through the
[GraalVM Reachability Metadata Repository](https://github.com/oracle/graalvm-reachability-metadata),
and the literal `Class.forName()`, `getResource()` and native calls in your own code.

## Detect orphan project classes

Room `*_Impl`, Dagger `*_Factory` and Moshi adapters are loaded by name, so no bytecode references
them. The plugin registers such a class when it is public, has a public no-arg constructor, and
your code references one of its supertypes. The build log prints `[orphan] <fqcn>` for each.

`detectOrphanProjectClasses` is on by default. `reflectionForProjectClasses = true` registers every
project class with a public no-arg constructor; use it only to unblock a build, since it grows the
image.

## Fill gaps with the tracing agent

Reflection driven by run-time values escapes the build-time analysis. Run the agent once before a
release and walk through every screen:

```shell
./gradlew runWithNativeAgent
```

The agent merges new entries into your `reachability-metadata.json` and keeps the ones you edited.
Commit that file. To keep it in another folder, set `graalvm { nativeImageConfigBaseDir }`. To spot
gaps earlier, see
[Catch missing registrations](/docs/performance/graalvm/configuration#catch-missing-registrations-in-the-dev-loop).

## Clean up manual entries

```shell
./gradlew cleanupGraalvmMetadata
# Also remove entries whose types are on no classpath
./gradlew cleanupGraalvmMetadata -Pnucleus.graalvm.cleanup.removeUnresolvable=true
# Report without rewriting the file
./gradlew cleanupGraalvmMetadata -Pnucleus.graalvm.cleanup.dryRun=true
```

The task removes the entries the generated metadata already covers and lists what it kept. A
`kept` entry is covered by nothing else, so check it.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

The plugin merges five sources, each passed through its own `-H:ConfigurationFileDirectories=`:

1. 29 metadata files in the plugin JAR, kept when their `matchPackages` are on the classpath
   (`filterGraalvmLibraryMetadata`). Headless builds drop the GUI packs.
2. The Reachability Metadata Repository, version `1.1.4` (`resolveGraalvmReachabilityMetadata`).
3. Platform metadata for `sun.awt.windows.*`, `sun.lwawt.macosx.*` or `sun.awt.X11.*`, Java2D,
   font managers, security providers and `main` (`generateGraalvmPlatformMetadata`).
4. A bytecode scan of the runtime classpath (`analyzeGraalvmStaticMetadata`). It also catches
   `MethodHandles.Lookup.findClass()`, JNI callbacks and `@Serializable` companions. The orphan
   detector reads the app's JVM target folders, such as `desktopMainClasses`.
5. Metadata inside `nucleus.graalvm-runtime`: resource globs (`**/*.svg`, `**/*.ttf`,
   `composeResources/**`, `META-INF/services/**`, …), `-H:+SharedArenaSupport`, and AWT font and
   splash-screen substitutions.

`cleanupGraalvmMetadata` compares your file with sources 1 to 4. It always drops the Kotlin
phantoms the agent records (`kotlin.Any`, `FunctionN`, …) and never drops types under the
`exactReachabilityMetadata` packages.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## What's next

- [Tasks and CI](/docs/performance/graalvm/tasks-ci): the full GraalVM task graph.
- [Configuration](/docs/performance/graalvm/configuration): every `graalvm { }` property.

# Tasks and CI

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/performance/graalvm/tasks-ci

The Gradle tasks the Nucleus plugin adds for GraalVM Native Image, where their output lands, and how to build on each OS in GitHub Actions.

The GraalVM tasks mirror the JVM pipeline, plus one packaging task per installer format.

## Gradle tasks

| Task | JVM counterpart | Description |
|------|-----------------|-------------|
| `runGraalvmNative` | `run` | Dev loop: quick-build (`-Ob`) with [exact reachability](/docs/performance/graalvm/configuration#catch-missing-registrations-in-the-dev-loop), then runs the binary. |
| `createGraalvmNativeDistributable` | `createDistributable` | Builds the app folder for the current OS, without an installer. |
| `runGraalvmNativeDistributable` | `runDistributable` | Builds with the configured optimization and runs the app folder. |
| `packageGraalvmNativeDistributionForCurrentOS` | `packageDistributionForCurrentOS` | Packages every configured format for the current OS. |

### Metadata, installers and helpers

| Task | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `packageGraalvm<Format>` | One installer per format in `nativeDistributions.targetFormats`, named after the enum constant: `TargetFormat.Deb` gives `packageGraalvmDeb`. |
| `runWithNativeAgent` | Runs the app under the tracing agent to record metadata. See [Automatic metadata](/docs/performance/graalvm/automatic-metadata#fill-gaps-with-the-tracing-agent). |
| `cleanupGraalvmMetadata` | Removes manual entries the generated metadata already covers. |
| `runWithPgoInstrument` | Records a PGO profile. Oracle GraalVM only. |

Installers need no Node.js on the build machine: the plugin downloads it. See
`nativeDistributions { nodejs { } }` in the [Gradle DSL reference](/docs/reference/gradle-dsl#nodejs).

`packageGraalvmDeb` fails unless `nativeDistributions { homepage }` is set.

## Output layout

The app folder lands in `build/compose/binaries/main/graalvm-app/`: a signed `<app>.app` on macOS,
`<app>.exe` on Windows, `<app>` on Linux, with the Nucleus JNI libraries next to the executable.
Installers land in `build/compose/binaries/main/graalvm-<format>/`, for example `graalvm-dmg`.

## Build in CI with GitHub Actions

You cannot cross-compile a native image. Run a matrix over the three OSes and set up each runner
with the `setup-nucleus` action:

```yaml title=".github/workflows/graalvm-release.yml"
name: GraalVM release

on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]

jobs:
  graalvm:
    name: GraalVM - ${{ matrix.name }}
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 60
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          - { name: Linux x64,   os: ubuntu-latest,  task: packageGraalvmDeb }
          - { name: macOS ARM64, os: macos-latest,   task: packageGraalvmDmg }
          - { name: Windows x64, os: windows-latest, task: packageGraalvmNsis }

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Nucleus
        uses: NucleusFramework/Nucleus/.github/actions/setup-nucleus@main
        with:
          graalvm: 'true'
          setup-gradle: 'true'

      - name: Build the native package
        run: ./gradlew :myapp:${{ matrix.task }} --no-daemon

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: graalvm-${{ runner.os }}
          path: myapp/build/compose/binaries/**/graalvm-*/**
```

- `graalvm: 'true'` installs Xcode tooling or MSVC and caches the GraalVM toolchain. Keep the
  `graalvm-version` and `graalvm-distribution` inputs (defaults `25i4`, `community`) in line with
  your `toolchain { }` block: they are cache keys.
- `setup-gradle: 'true'` caches Gradle dependencies and outputs. The `native-image` step itself
  takes 5 to 15 minutes per platform.

`setup-nucleus` no longer installs Node.js, and the `setup-node` input is gone. `node-version` only
feeds the cache key and should match `nodejs { version }`.

## Debug missing reflection at run time

Run the binary from a terminal. A missing registration shows up as `ClassNotFoundException`,
`NoSuchFieldException` or, under `runGraalvmNative`, `MissingReflectionRegistrationError`. Run
`./gradlew runWithNativeAgent` through the failing path, then rebuild.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- `packageGraalvmNative` is the internal assembler behind these tasks: it compiles the image and
  lays out the binary, JNI, Skiko and AWT libraries, icons and `appResources`.
- `filterGraalvmLibraryMetadata`, `resolveGraalvmReachabilityMetadata`,
  `generateGraalvmPlatformMetadata` and `analyzeGraalvmStaticMetadata` run on every native build.
- The quick-build mode is a task input, so switching between `runGraalvmNative` and the
  distributable tasks recompiles.
- The image compiles from a copy of the uber JAR without the Nucleus JNI libraries.
  `NativeLibraryLoader` loads them from next to the executable and never extracts them. See
  [Native library loader](/docs/performance/native-library-loader).
- Node.js lands in `<gradle-user-home>/nucleus/nodejs` for electron-builder.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## What's next

- [Configuration](/docs/performance/graalvm/configuration): the `graalvm { }` DSL.
- [Automatic metadata](/docs/performance/graalvm/automatic-metadata): the metadata behind these tasks.
- [CI/CD](/docs/packaging/ci-cd): the full release workflow with signing and publishing.

# AOT cache

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/performance/aot-cache

Generate a Project Leyden AOT cache at build time and ship it in every installer, so the JVM skips most of its warmup at launch.

The Nucleus plugin can generate a [Project Leyden](https://openjdk.org/projects/leyden/) AOT cache
during a training run of your app and ship it in every installer. At launch the JVM reuses the
recorded class loading and profiles, so the first window appears sooner. The runtime API comes
with `nucleus-application`.

## Enable the cache

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
nucleus.application {
    mainClass = "com.example.MainKt"
    nativeDistributions {
        enableAotCache = true
    }
}
```

AOT cache generation needs JDK 25 or later as the packaging JDK. An older JDK fails the build.

The plugin runs the app in training mode after `createDistributable`, then ships `app.aot` in every
installer and wires it into the launcher.

## Write a training run

The JVM writes the cache when the training process exits, so your app must exit on its own, with
code 0, within 300 s. After that the plugin kills it. Inside `nucleusApplication`, arm the exit timer with
`aotTraining`:

```kotlin
fun main(args: Array<String>) = nucleusApplication(args) {
    // No-op outside training. Calls exitApplication() after 45 seconds.
    aotTraining(duration = 45.seconds)

    if (isAotTraining) {
        // Each screen the run touches adds profiled methods to the cache
        preloadNavigationScreens()
        preloadFontsAndImages()
    }

    DecoratedWindow(onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication, title = "MyApp") {
        App()
    }
}
```

Walk through the screens a real session opens: more coverage gives a shorter cold start.

Without `nucleusApplication`, check `AotRuntime.isTraining()` and call `exitProcess(0)` yourself
once the run is done.

## Pin the platform and JDK

A cache only loads on the platform and JDK build that produced it. Build on each target platform,
typically in a CI matrix, and release a fresh cache with each app version. The plugin trains with
the JDK it bundles, including OpenJDK 27 when
[`lastJdk`](/docs/performance/startup#package-with-the-latest-jdk) is on.

### Choose a compatibility profile

Set `nativeDistributions { aotCache { compatibility } }`:

| `AotCacheCompatibility` | Behavior |
|-------------------------|----------|
| `COMPATIBILITY` | No cached machine code. Runs on any CPU of the architecture. The default. |
| `NATIVE` | Keeps machine code for the build CPU, for a small startup gain. A user CPU with fewer instruction-set extensions crashes with `SIGILL` or `EXCEPTION_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION`. JDK 27 checks this at load time; the plugin warns below 27. |

To measure the gain, time a build with `enableAotCache = false` against one with it on, same JDK,
from process spawn to the first frame.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- The training run records into `app.aot` with `-XX:AOTCacheOutput`. The launcher gets
  `-XX:AOTCache=$APPDIR/app.aot`.
- The plugin sets `-Dnucleus.aot.mode=training` for the training run. The shipped launcher sets
  nothing, so a packaged app reports `OFF` unless you add `-Dnucleus.aot.mode=runtime` to
  `jvmArgs`.
- On Linux without `DISPLAY`, the plugin starts Xvfb for the training run.

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## API reference

| Gradle property | Default | Notes |
|-----------------|---------|-------|
| `nativeDistributions.enableAotCache` | `false` | Shorthand for `aotCache { enabled }`. |
| `aotCache.enabled` | `false` | Trains, bundles, and wires the cache into the launcher. |
| `aotCache.compatibility` | `COMPATIBILITY` | See [Choose a compatibility profile](#choose-a-compatibility-profile). |
| `aotCache.extraTrainingJvmArgs` | empty | Extra JVM arguments for the training run only. |

| Kotlin API | Notes |
|------------|-------|
| `AotRuntime.mode()` / `aotMode` | `AotRuntimeMode.OFF`, `TRAINING` or `RUNTIME` |
| `AotRuntime.isTraining()` / `isAotTraining` | `true` during a training run |
| `AotRuntime.isRuntime()` / `isAotRuntime` | `true` when `nucleus.aot.mode` is `runtime` |
| `aotTraining(duration, onTimeout)` | Exit timer, `nucleusApplication` scope. Defaults: 15 s, `exitApplication()`. Only the first call arms it. |

`AotRuntime` lives in `dev.nucleusframework.aot.runtime`.

## What's next

- [Startup optimization](/docs/performance/startup): the `nucleusOptimization` pack, which pairs with the AOT cache.
- [GraalVM Native Image](/docs/performance/graalvm): the alternative for the smallest binary and memory use.
- [CI/CD](/docs/packaging/ci-cd): build a per-platform cache in a CI matrix.

# Native code in Kotlin

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/performance/native-code

Write platform code in Kotlin/Native and call it from the JVM as a Kotlin API. The NucleusNativeAccess plugin generates the FFM bridge, the JVM proxies and the GraalVM metadata.

NucleusNativeAccess lets you write code in Kotlin/Native and call it from the JVM as a regular
Kotlin class, with no JNI and no C. Use it for a platform API that no Nucleus module covers.

NucleusNativeAccess ships from [`NucleusFramework/NucleusNativeAccess`](https://github.com/NucleusFramework/NucleusNativeAccess)
as the Gradle plugin `dev.nucleusframework.nna`, with its own version. It needs JDK 22 or later at
run time (25 recommended), Kotlin 2.3.20 and Gradle 9.1.

## Create the native module

Put the native code in its own Gradle module, without the Compose compiler plugin: Compose does
not support the extra Kotlin/Native compilations the bridge needs.

```kotlin title="native/build.gradle.kts"
plugins {
    kotlin("multiplatform") version "2.3.20"
    id("dev.nucleusframework.nna") version "<version>"
}

kotlin {
    jvmToolchain(25)
    jvm()
    linuxX64() // or macosArm64(), mingwX64()
}

kotlinNativeExport {
    nativeLibName = "mylib" // libmylib.so, libmylib.dylib or mylib.dll
    buildType = "release"   // "release" (default) or "debug"
}
```

Then add `implementation(project(":native"))` to the app's `jvmMain` dependencies. Nucleus
already passes `--enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED` to `run`, the packaged app and native images.

## Write the native class

Only the public API crosses the boundary:

```kotlin title="native/src/nativeMain/kotlin/com/example/Calculator.kt"
package com.example

class Calculator(initial: Int = 0) {
    private var acc = initial

    fun add(value: Int): Int { acc += value; return acc }
    val current: Int get() = acc
}
```

## Call it from the JVM

The generated proxy has the same shape and implements `AutoCloseable`. Closing it releases the
native object:

```kotlin title="app/src/jvmMain/kotlin/com/example/Main.kt"
Calculator(0).use { calc ->
    calc.add(5)
    println(calc.current) // 5
}
```

## Supported types

Primitives, `String`, `ByteArray`, collections, data classes, enums, nullable types, objects,
`suspend fun`, `Flow<T>`, lambdas and exceptions (rethrown as `KotlinNativeException`) all cross
the bridge. Classes, inheritance, interfaces, sealed classes, companion objects, default parameters
and extensions on your own classes carry over.

The bridge does not support:

- Generics. Use concrete types.
- An interface or sealed class as a return type. Return the concrete class.
- Operator overloading and infix functions.
- Extension functions on standard library types.
- `ByteArray` inside collections, data class fields or callback parameters.
- Subclassing a native class from the JVM.
- Kotlin/Native-only types such as `CPointer` in the public API.

## Wrap a C library

Declare `cinterop` bindings in the native module, wrap them in a Kotlin class in `nativeMain`, and
keep C types such as `CPointer` inside that class:

```kotlin title="native/build.gradle.kts"
kotlin {
    linuxX64().compilations["main"].cinterops {
        val libnotify by creating { defFile(project.file("src/nativeInterop/cinterop/libnotify.def")) }
    }
}
```

```kotlin title="native/src/nativeMain/kotlin/com/example/LinuxDesktop.kt"
class LinuxDesktop {
    fun sendNotification(title: String, body: String, icon: String): Boolean {
        notify_init("MyApp")
        val n = notify_notification_new(title, body, icon) ?: return false
        return notify_notification_show(n, null) != 0
    }
}
```

## Build a native image

The plugin writes the GraalVM metadata for you. A native image cannot extract the library from the
JAR, so ship `libmylib` next to the executable.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- The plugin reads the public API of `nativeMain`, generates `@CName` bridge functions that track
  each object with a `StableRef`, and JVM proxies that call them through FFM downcalls.
- The library ships in the JAR under `kne/native/{os}-{arch}/`. At run time the proxy tries
  `java.library.path`, then extracts to `~/.cache/kne/`, then the loader lookup native images need.
- A `Cleaner` releases native objects whose proxies you never closed.
- GraalVM metadata lives under `META-INF/native-image/kne/{libName}/` (`reflect-config.json`,
  `resource-config.json`, `reachability-metadata.json`). See [Automatic metadata](/docs/performance/graalvm/automatic-metadata).
- This loader is separate from the [Nucleus native library loader](/docs/performance/native-library-loader).

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## What's next

- [Native library loader](/docs/performance/native-library-loader): how Nucleus modules load their JNI libraries.
- [GraalVM Native Image](/docs/performance/graalvm): compile the app to a native binary.

# Native library loader

URL: https://nucleusframework.dev/en/docs/performance/native-library-loader

How Nucleus modules load their JNI libraries, from the folder next to a packaged app, the library path, or a content-addressed cache you can relocate.

`NativeLibraryLoader` loads the JNI libraries of Nucleus modules, and of your own JNI bridge, in a
packaged app, a fat JAR or an IDE run. It lives in `core-runtime`, which comes with
`nucleus-application`.

## Load a library

```kotlin
import dev.nucleusframework.core.runtime.NativeLibraryLoader

private val loaded: Boolean = NativeLibraryLoader.load(
    "nucleus_systemcolor",
    NativeWindowsSystemColorBridge::class.java,
)
```

`load` returns `true` once the library is in the process, and `false` when no binary exists for
this platform or loading failed. It does not throw: treat `false` as "not available". A second
call with the same name returns `true` without reloading.

| Parameter | Default | Role |
|-----------|---------|------|
| `libraryName` | required | Base name without `lib` or extension, for example `"nucleus_systemcolor"` |
| `callerClass` | required | A class from the JAR that holds the library |
| `resourcePrefix` | `"/nucleus/native"` | Root folder inside the JAR |
| `sidecarFiles` | `emptyList()` | Helper files extracted next to the library before it loads |

Put the binaries in the JAR under `{resourcePrefix}/{os}-{arch}/`, with `os` one of `darwin`,
`linux`, `win32` and `arch` one of `x64`, `aarch64`:

```text
/nucleus/native/darwin-aarch64/libnucleus_systemcolor.dylib
/nucleus/native/linux-x64/libnucleus_systemcolor.so
/nucleus/native/win32-x64/nucleus_systemcolor.dll
```

Packaged apps no longer carry Nucleus JNI libraries inside their JARs: the plugin ships them next
to the app. Code that read them as classpath resources in a packaged app must load them through
`NativeLibraryLoader`. See [Migrate from 2.x](/docs/migrate/from-2.x).

## Sidecar files

Pass helper DLLs that the library needs next to it, as named in the JAR resource folder:

```kotlin
NativeLibraryLoader.load(
    "sample_tao_webview",
    SampleWebViewWindowsBridge::class.java,
    sidecarFiles = listOf("WebView2Loader.dll"),
)
```

## Relocate the cache

Fat JARs, IDE runs and distributions built without the plugin extract libraries to a per-user
cache: `~/Library/Caches/nucleus/native/` on macOS, `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/nucleus/native/` (or
`~/.cache/…`) on Linux, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\nucleus\native\` on Windows. Apps packaged by the plugin
extract nothing.

To move the root, set `nucleus.native.cacheDir` in `jvmArgs`. It covers libraries that load before
your code runs:

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
nucleus.application {
    jvmArgs("-Dnucleus.native.cacheDir=/var/lib/myapp/native")
}
```

The JVM does not expand `${user.home}` there. For a path computed at run time, set it from code
before the first native load:

```kotlin
fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    NativeLibraryLoader.cacheDirectory = Path(System.getProperty("user.home"), ".myapp", "native")
    nucleusApplication(args) { /* ... */ }
}
```

The system property wins over `cacheDirectory`. A later assignment is ignored with a warning. Do
not point the cache at the install directory or inside a macOS `.app`: a standard user cannot
write there, and writing inside the bundle breaks its signature.

## JNI exceptions in the logs

When a Kotlin listener throws inside a native callback, Nucleus logs it as a `WARNING` from the
`dev.nucleusframework.core.runtime.JniExceptionReporter` logger, even when
`allowNucleusRuntimeLogging` is off. Before 3.0 these exceptions disappeared.

## Debugging

| Situation | What to check |
|-----------|---------------|
| A module reports `isAvailable == false` | Does the dependency JAR contain `/nucleus/native/<os>-<arch>/` for your platform, or does the packaged app folder contain the library? |
| Load fails after an upgrade in an IDE or fat-JAR run | Delete the cache root and relaunch. |
| A warning says the cache directory is unusable | The configured directory cannot be written. The loader moved on to the next candidate. |
| `Failed to load … native library` | Enable `FINE` logging for `dev.nucleusframework.core.runtime.NativeLibraryLoader`. |

In app code, check a module's `isAvailable` flag instead of calling `NativeLibraryLoader`.

<Accordions>
<Accordion title="Under the hood">

- Load order: the `nucleus.native.libraryPath` directory (set by the plugin's launcher), then
  `System.loadLibrary` on `java.library.path` (sandboxed store builds, GraalVM native images), then
  extraction from the JAR.
- jpackage builds keep the libraries in `$APPDIR` next to Skiko; native images keep them next to
  the executable (`Contents/MacOS/` on macOS). Only libraries listed in a Nucleus module's
  `META-INF/nucleus/native-libraries/` manifest move; yours stay in their JARs.
- A missing resource logs at `FINE` and returns `false`, so a macOS-only module stays silent on Linux.
- Cache layout: `<root>/<os>-<arch>/<fingerprint>/<file>`. The fingerprint comes from the JAR
  entry's CRC-32 and size (size and mtime for `file:` URLs); sidecars share it. Extraction writes
  a temp file and renames it.
- Cache root order: `nucleus.native.cacheDir`, then `cacheDirectory`, then the platform default.
  The loader checks each with a real write probe and falls through on failure. An empty or
  relative `XDG_CACHE_HOME` or `LOCALAPPDATA` is ignored.
- The JNI exception message is `Native JNI callback cleared a pending Kotlin exception`, logged
  through `java.util.logging` with the throwable attached.
- [Native code in Kotlin](/docs/performance/native-code) has its own, independent loader
  (`~/.cache/kne/`, `kne/native/`).

</Accordion>
</Accordions>

## What's next

- [Modules](/docs/concepts/modules): `core-runtime` and the rest of the module map.
- [Troubleshooting](/docs/reference/troubleshooting): packaging and runtime failures.
